# AOTC, LLC (Ads of the Century)

> AOTC, LLC (Ads of the Century) is a mobile digital billboard company: LED billboard trucks, planned and run across the United States from its home base in Chicago. It specializes in rotational campaigns (10-second rotations shared by up to six brands, never two competitors in the same rotation; exclusive single-brand bookings quoted separately), routes planned by daypart around the audience, creative designed in-house, GPS-tracked routes, and photos of the ad on the street after every run.

Also known as: AOTC, AOTC LLC, Ads of the Century, Advertisements of the Century, AOTC Media, adsofthecentury.net

- Phone: (773) 708-1400 (call or text, 24/7)
- Email: info@adsofthecentury.net
- Home base: Chicago, Illinois. Campaigns nationwide.
- Get a route plan and quote: the Book Now button on any page of https://adsofthecentury.net/, usually answered the same day

## Key facts
- Screens: full-size LED screens on both sides and the rear carry the full ad: sides 11.76 x 6.30 ft (1920 x 1029 px), rear 6.71 x 6.30 ft (1080 x 1014 px). AOTC's own truck adds a front screen, 6.71 x 3.36 ft (1280 x 641 px). Files: JPG, PNG or MP4.
- Standard bookings are rotational: 10-second rotations shared by up to six brands, with no competing brand in the same rotation; share of voice runs from about 15% to 100%. Exclusive bookings put one brand alone on the truck and are quoted separately.
- Delivery record: GPS-tracked routes and photos of the ad on the street after every run. Response is measured with QR codes, promo codes, vanity URLs or call tracking.
- Free tool: the Display Studio (https://adsofthecentury.net/display.html) previews your design on the real truck before you book.
- Clients see their truck live in the Golden Ticket route room.
- Cities where AOTC, LLC has run its own campaigns: Chicago (the Loop, Wrigleyville, River North, Chinatown, Fulton Market, Grant Park), Bedford Park, IL; Hammond, Whiting and East Chicago, IN; the I-94 corridor in Northwest Indiana; Michigan City, IN; and New Buffalo, MI.
- As seen on: WGN-TV, NBC 5 Chicago, ABC7 Chicago, FOX 32 Chicago, Telemundo Chicago, The Times of Northwest Indiana (nwi.com).

- Wendy's (Quick service · Grand opening, Bedford Park, IL): A full-motion route through the corridors that feed the store, timed to meal and commute windows, then the truck out front on opening day with the mascots, the opening message on every screen and a QR code for the offer. Opening week landed like an event, not a soft open. The trade area saw Wendy's on the days that mattered most. [https://adsofthecentury.net/grand-opening-mobile-billboards.html#wendys]

A company most people never see became the brand in front of the season's first crowd, and in front of the city all week. [https://adsofthecentury.net/game-day-mobile-billboards.html#american-precision-services]
- USW Local 7-1 (Labor · Public awareness, Indiana to downtown Chicago): Four activations: a community parade in Hammond, two hours circling the BP facility, a solidarity march from East Chicago through Hammond and Whiting to BP's downtown Chicago offices, and Festival of the Lakes. One message carried through four public moments, four cities and two states, and onto the local news. [https://adsofthecentury.net/political-mobile-billboards.html#usw-local-7-1]
- Uncle Sam's Fireworks (Retail · Seasonal peak, I-94 Exit 68B, Indiana): A placement beside the traffic stream with Exit 68B in the same view, so the offer and the turn arrived together. When a storm closure sent traffic toward that exit, the truck was already there. The only fireworks message drivers met before the exit. Fixed billboards couldn't follow the detour. The truck didn't have to. [https://adsofthecentury.net/grand-opening-mobile-billboards.html#uncle-sams-fireworks]

Then a two-day, three-state run: New Buffalo, Michigan City Premium Outlets and Grant Park during Sueños. Elevated Exotics came back for a second, bigger campaign: from a 24-hour turnaround to a three-state route in front of a 100,000-plus festival audience. [https://adsofthecentury.net/led-screen-truck-rental.html#elevated-exotics]

April's portrait, phone number and "Buy, Sell, Invest, Lease" on every screen. She didn't share the screen. She owned it, from the daytime crowds to the Loop after dark. [https://adsofthecentury.net/downtown-mobile-billboards.html#realty-of-america]
- HCDS Mental Health (Nonprofit mental health · Sueños weekend, Downtown Chicago): Three consecutive days of downtown routes with bright orange creative: the services, insurance accepted, and a phone number plus a QR code for a direct next step. The message stayed legible against the downtown architecture, from sidewalk and roadway, with two easy ways to reach them. [https://adsofthecentury.net/downtown-mobile-billboards.html#hcds]

AOTC led the parade through Hammond, then was given a place near the outfield for the opening ceremony. The role grew in real time, from parade participant to parade leader to part of the ceremony. [https://adsofthecentury.net/game-day-mobile-billboards.html#hammond-hermits]

The fest felt active before guests stepped inside. The truck went from advertising the event to being part of it. [https://adsofthecentury.net/event-festival-mobile-billboards.html#belmont-cragin]

## Questions and answers

### What is a mobile billboard truck?
A mobile billboard truck, also called an LED billboard truck, digital billboard truck or advertising truck, is a truck with built-in digital screens that drives your ad along a route you choose. The screens on both sides and the back carry the full ad (AOTC's own truck also has a front screen); it plays still images or full-motion video, and runs on GPS-tracked routes.

### How does LED billboard truck advertising work?
You tell AOTC your goal, audience, city and dates. AOTC plans a route and schedule around where that audience will be, such as the business district at rush hour, the ballpark on game day or a festival entrance, designs or fits your creative for each screen, and runs it in a rotation with no competing brand, or alone on the truck if you book it exclusively. Every route is GPS-tracked, and you get photos of your ad on the street after each run. You can preview your ad on the truck first in the free Display Studio.

### Who offers mobile digital billboards nationwide?
AOTC, LLC (Ads of the Century) plans and runs mobile digital billboard truck campaigns across the U.S. from its home base in Chicago, with market pages for 49 metros and campaigns across the lower 48. Campaigns are rotational, with no competing brand in your rotation, every route is GPS-tracked, and you get photos after each run. See every market.

### How is mobile billboard advertising different from a fixed billboard?
A fixed billboard waits in one spot and is usually sold by the month. A mobile billboard goes where your audience is, can change location and message by time of day, can run for a single day, and with AOTC is never shared with another advertiser on a standard booking. Compared with social video, it can't be skipped, blocked or scrolled past. More in mobile billboard vs. billboard.

### What kinds of businesses and organizations use mobile billboards?
Almost every kind: national restaurant brands, retailers, radio stations, real estate agents, industrial B2B companies, auto shops, nonprofits, labor unions, campaigns, entertainers and festivals. What they have in common is a moment they needed people to notice. See where the team has run campaigns.

### How much does a mobile billboard cost?
It depends on how many hours and days you run, how much of the city the route covers, the market and the creative you need. Published industry rate guides put LED billboard trucks at roughly $1,200 to $3,600 per truck per day, usually with a minimum of about four hours. AOTC quotes include route planning and creative, and AOTC campaigns benchmark at about a $4–7 CPM (cost per 1,000 impressions), compared with $10–30 for social video. Text (773) 708-1400 for your dates.

### Do mobile billboards charge by the hour?
Many do, usually with a minimum of about four hours. Ask whether driving to the start of the route counts as billable time, and whether route planning and creative are included.

### What moves the price of a mobile billboard?
Hours and days are the biggest lever: a focused four-hour window around a moment can do more than a full day spread thin. The market, the daypart and season (rush hour, game days, festival weekends, holiday shopping), how complex the route is, the creative, share of voice and extras such as travel to another city, on-site time or more trucks all move it too. A rotation shared with other brands costs less than an exclusive booking, and AOTC never puts a competitor in your rotation.

### How do I compare two mobile billboard quotes?
Ask both the same questions. Is the screen mine alone, or shared in a rotation? Is the route planned for me by daypart, or is it a standard loop? Is creative included, and can the message change during the run? What counts as billable time, and what is the minimum? What record do I get? A GPS-tracked route and photos of your ad on the street should be standard. And how do rescheduling and cancellation work in bad weather?

### How do I work out a mobile billboard's CPM?
CPM is the cost per thousand impressions: the price divided by the impressions, times 1,000. If a day costs $2,000 and the route delivers an estimated 400,000 impression opportunities, the CPM is $5. Street impressions are estimates, so ask how any number was worked out and treat it as a planning figure, not a guarantee.

### Is a mobile billboard cheaper than a regular billboard?
For a short, date-driven campaign, usually yes in total spend, because you can buy one day or one event instead of a four-week period. Over a full year on one road, a fixed board can cost less per month. Compare by cost per thousand impressions and by what each one can actually do for your goal.

### What's included in an AOTC quote?
The route plan, the hours, still-image creative designed in-house, a rotation with no competing brand, a GPS-tracked route and photos of your ad on the street after every run. Motion design and extras such as other cities or on-site time are quoted with the plan. Send the city, the dates, the hours, who you want to reach and whether you have creative, and AOTC comes back with a route plan and a quote, usually the same day.

### How long does an LED truck campaign run?
As long as the goal needs. A single-day activation can own a grand opening, a festival or a game day. A multi-day flight builds the repetition that turns recognition into recall, and longer runs keep a brand present in a neighborhood. AOTC schedules the hours and days your audience is actually on the street.

### How far in advance should I book an advertising truck?
As early as you can, especially for holidays, festivals, trade shows and summer weekends, when dates fill quickly, and earlier still for campaigns outside Chicago or across several cities. AOTC has also turned campaigns around fast for real deadlines, including an event booked the day before, so text (773) 708-1400 with your date to check availability.

### Is the truck available for private events?
Yes. The four LED screens also work as an event screen for brand activations, festivals, corporate events, watch parties, movie nights, birthdays and memorials. At an Elevated Exotics event in New Buffalo, the screens ran movies and video games live. See LED screen truck rental.

### Can AOTC run a nationwide mobile billboard campaign?
Yes. AOTC is based in Chicago and plans and runs mobile billboard campaigns in markets across the U.S.: multi-city launches on the same day, tours and roadshows that follow your schedule, and trade-show and event circuits. Every market runs to the same standard, with one plan and one point of contact for the whole campaign.

### Which cities does AOTC cover?
AOTC, LLC has market pages for 49 metros, including New York, Los Angeles, Dallas–Fort Worth, Houston, Atlanta, Miami, Washington, DC, Las Vegas, San Francisco and Chicago, its home base, and plans campaigns anywhere in the lower 48. Don't see your city? Text the city and the date to (773) 708-1400. See all markets.

### Where is AOTC based?
Chicago, Illinois. The home region includes the Chicago suburbs, Northwest Indiana and Southwest Michigan, and AOTC has run single campaigns across three states in two days. Campaigns in other markets are planned by the same team, to the same standard.

### Are mobile billboards legal in every city?
Not everywhere, and not in the same way. Some cities regulate or restrict advertising vehicles, and venues set their own rules on their property. AOTC checks the current rules for your format, city and route before it quotes, and tells you up front what will and won't work.

### Can I choose where a mobile billboard drives?
Yes. Every AOTC route is planned for one client. Name the streets, neighborhoods, venues or events, and AOTC builds a loop and schedule around when your audience is there.

### Can a mobile billboard target a specific neighborhood or event?
Yes. A route can be as tight as a few blocks around a new location or a festival entrance, or as wide as several neighborhoods in a day. See event and festival advertising and downtown routes.

### Can a mobile billboard run near a stadium on game day?
Yes. AOTC has run Cubs Opening Day routes through Wrigleyville for American Precision Services, timed to pre-game arrivals and post-game crowds, and plans the same timing around stadiums in any city. See game-day advertising.

### How do you plan routes around my target audience?
AOTC starts with who you need to reach and where their day happens: the corridors they commute, the blocks they walk, and the venues and events they go to. From there it builds a loop and schedule that keeps the truck in front of that audience at the hours they're there: wide coverage for a launch, tighter repeated loops when a date matters. More in how to plan a campaign.

### Do you run at night?
Yes, and night is often when the screens do their best work: full-motion LED stays bright after dark, when fixed boards fade. Evening routes suit nightlife, entertainment, events and any brand whose customers are out after work.

### What artwork or video files does an LED billboard truck need?
A JPG, PNG or MP4 for each screen: 1920 × 1029 px for the two side screens, 1080 × 1014 for the back and 1280 × 641 for the front. No artwork? AOTC designs it in-house, or preview your own design on the truck for free.

### How big are the screens?
Each side screen is 11.76 × 6.30 ft and the back screen is 6.71 × 6.30 ft, so the full ad reads from both sidewalks and the traffic behind. AOTC's own truck adds a front screen above the cab, 6.71 × 3.36 ft.

### What if I don't have creative ready?
Then we make it. AOTC designs creative in-house, and much of what runs on our screens was designed by us for the client. Bring an idea, a logo or nothing at all, or mock one up yourself in the Display Studio.

### Can I change my message during the campaign?
Yes. The screens are digital, so creative can change between dayparts, between cities on a tour, add a limited-time offer mid-run, or switch from "Opening Saturday" to "Now open" without a reprint.

### Do I share the screen with other advertisers?
Yes, on a standard booking, and that's what AOTC specializes in. Up to six brands take 10-second turns on the screens, never two from the same category, which keeps the price down; your share of voice runs from about 15% to 100%. If you want the truck to yourself, an exclusive booking puts only your brand on every screen. Your quote always says which one you're getting.

### How do you measure a mobile billboard campaign?
In two parts: delivery and response. Delivery: every route is GPS-tracked, and after each run you get photos of your ad on the street. Response is measured the way you'd measure any channel: put a QR code, promo code, vanity URL or tracked phone number in the creative, then compare traffic, calls, sales or branded search in the route areas against the weeks before.

### How do I know the truck actually ran?
Every AOTC route is GPS-tracked, and after each run you get photos of your ad on the street, ready to share with your team or your client. Clients can also follow their truck live in the Golden Ticket route room.

### What kind of results can I expect?
That depends on your offer, your market and the moment you choose, which is why every AOTC plan starts with the outcome you want. Clients have used routes to fill grand openings, keep a cause in public view, put a radio station in front of a festival crowd and win a holiday weekend at a highway exit. Put a code or link on the screen and you can count the response yourself.

## Guides

### Mobile billboard vs. traditional billboard (https://adsofthecentury.net/mobile-billboard-vs-billboard.html)
Key takeaways:
A fixed billboard is one location, usually sold in four-week periods; digital boards rotate several advertisers.
A mobile billboard truck goes to the audience and can run for a single day, event or daypart.
AOTC rotations share the screens among up to six brands, never two competitors; exclusive bookings give one brand 100%.
Fixed boards win for always-on presence on one road; trucks win for moments, neighborhoods, events and launches.
Measure either one the same way: QR codes, promo codes, vanity URLs or call tracking against a baseline.
Side by side
Fixed billboard Digital billboard LED billboard truck
Location One spot, chosen from available inventory One spot Any streets you choose, and it moves
Minimum Usually a four-week period Usually weeks Hours or a single day
Share of the screen Yours Rotates with other advertisers in short slots Rotates up to six brands, no competitors; or yours alone on an exclusive booking
Message changes Reprint and reinstall Possible Any time, by daypart, neighborhood or city
Viewing height Elevated, read from the road Elevated Eye level, read from sidewalk and road
At night Lit, if the board is lit Bright Bright, full-motion
Best for Always-on presence on a major road Frequent message updates on one road Launches, events, game days, neighborhoods, causes
When a fixed billboard wins
If your customers pass the same stretch of highway every day and you want to be there all year, a fixed board is efficient. Think of a hospital, a car dealer near an interchange, or a destination with a single main approach. Long-term contracts make the monthly cost predictable, and the board never takes a day off.
When a mobile billboard wins
When the moment matters more than the location. A truck goes to the audience at the hour it's there: the business district at rush hour, the ballpark on Opening Day, the festival gate, the convention hotels during show week. It can run for one day, change its message between morning and night, and appear in five neighborhoods or three cities in a week. And because it's at eye level and moving, people look, and often film.
It also wins where fixed inventory doesn't exist: dense downtown streets, residential neighborhoods, outside a specific building, or anywhere zoning keeps new boards out.
Static truck, LED truck or wrap?
Static poster truck Vehicle wrap LED billboard truck
The message One printed poster per flight Printed onto the vehicle Full-motion video and stills
Changes New print New wrap Instant, no reprint
Night Depends on lighting Weak Strongest after dark
Route Planned Wherever the vehicle goes Planned by daypart
Using both
Many brands layer the two: a fixed board for steady presence on the highway, and a truck for the moments that matter, such as the opening weekend, the big game or the trade show. The truck adds frequency in the exact places the fixed board can't reach, for the days it counts most.
How to measure either one
Measure the response, not just the exposure. Put a QR code, promo code, vanity URL or tracked phone number on the creative, and compare visits, calls, sales or branded search in the target area against the weeks before. For a truck, ask for the GPS-tracked route and photos from each run, so you know exactly where and when it ran. More in how to plan a campaign .

### How to plan a mobile billboard campaign (https://adsofthecentury.net/how-to-plan-a-mobile-billboard-campaign.html)
Key takeaways:
Start with one goal and the moment your audience is concentrated.
Plan the route by daypart around where the audience actually spends each hour.
Design big and simple: people read a moving screen in two or three seconds.
Add a QR code, promo code or call-tracking number so response can be counted.
Run it with a GPS-tracked route and photos, then compare results with your baseline.
1. Set one goal
Decide what the campaign has to do: fill an opening weekend, drive booth traffic, build name recognition before a vote, sell out an event, or keep a cause in public view. One goal shapes every other decision, from the route to the words on the screen.
Write it as an outcome you could count: "300 coupon redemptions in opening week" is a plan; "awareness" is a hope.
2. Pick the moment
Mobile billboards are strongest when the audience is concentrated: an opening day, a game, a festival, a trade show, a holiday weekend, a hearing. Choose the dates and hours when the people you want are in the same few blocks.
If there's no event, use the daily rhythm: rush hour in the business district, lunch on the shopping streets, evenings in the nightlife district.
3. Map where your audience's day happens
List the corridors they commute, the blocks they walk, the venues they visit and the times they're there. Be specific: a neighborhood, a convention hotel, a stadium gate, a highway exit, a ZIP code.
Every AOTC market page breaks its city down this way, by daypart. See New York , Dallas–Fort Worth or Chicago .
4. Plan the route by daypart
Turn the map into loops and hours. Wide coverage builds reach for a launch; tight, repeated loops build frequency when a date matters. Check the city's rules for advertising vehicles, and any venue rules, before you lock the plan.
Goal Route shape Example
Launch Wide loops across the trade area, then saturation on the day A grand opening's countdown week
Event The way in, the perimeter, the way home A festival or game day
B2B Business districts and convention hotels at set hours A trade show week
Advocacy Specific wards, buildings and moments A hearing or election eve
5. Design for motion and distance
People read a truck in about three seconds, often while moving. Use one idea, few words, big type, high contrast and one call to action. Put the brand where it can't be missed and design each screen for its shape.
Sides: 1920 × 1029 px, the main canvas
Back: 1080 × 1014 px, nearly square, read by traffic behind
Front: 1280 × 641 px, above the cab
Motion catches the eye; a message that changes by daypart keeps it fresh. Preview your design on the truck before you approve it.
6. Add a way to count the response
Put a QR code, promo code, vanity URL or tracked phone number on the screens. Note your baseline first: visits, calls, sales, sign-ups or branded search in the target area for the weeks before.
Use a different code per city or per daypart if you want to know which part of the plan worked best.
7. Run it, record it, read the results
During the run, the route is GPS-tracked and photos of your ad on the street come back after each run. Afterwards, compare the response against your baseline, see which hours and places performed, and adjust the next flight.
Photos and video from the street are also content: clients post them, put them in decks and send them to partners.
How far ahead to start
As early as you can. Holidays, festivals, trade-show weeks and summer weekends fill first, and campaigns in several cities need time to plan each stop. Short deadlines are sometimes possible: AOTC has been on site in under 24 hours. Text (773) 708-1400 with the city and the date.
The AOTC planning checklist
One goal you can count
The dates and hours of the moment
The places your audience will be, by daypart
The city and venue rules, checked
Creative for each screen, previewed on the truck
A code or link to count the response, and a baseline
A GPS-tracked route and photos from every run

### Mobile billboard trends for 2026 and 2027 (https://adsofthecentury.net/mobile-billboard-trends.html)
Key takeaways:
Advertisers are buying moments (a game, an opening, a festival) instead of months.
Screens are designed to be filmed and shared, so out-of-home feeds social.
Messages change by neighborhood and hour on LED screens.
Buyers expect measurement they can check: GPS-tracked routes, photos and response codes.
Clients increasingly watch the campaign live, and the truck doubles as an event venue.
1. Moments, not months
Out-of-home used to be bought by the four-week period. More and more, it's bought by the moment: an opening day, a game, a festival weekend, a trade-show week, a vote. Mobile billboards fit that shift because they can run for a single day and go where the moment is.
What to do: start the plan from the calendar, not the inventory. Find the three days your audience is most concentrated and put the budget there.
2. Out-of-home that feeds social
A truck at eye level gets filmed. In downtown Chicago, a crowd stopped to film the American Precision Services truck at night. The street is now a content source: every run produces photos and video that brands post, share and put in front of people who were never on that block.
What to do: design creative that looks good in a phone's frame, and plan to use the photos from every run as content.
3. Messages that change by place and hour
Digital screens on a moving truck make it practical to say different things to different neighborhoods, dayparts and cities: a lunch offer at noon, a dinner offer at six, the city's name on each stop of a tour. Previews are getting personal too: upload a design to AOTC's free Display Studio and see it on the truck before you've spoken to anyone.
What to do: write one creative system with swappable parts, not one fixed ad.
4. Measurement buyers can check
Buyers are more skeptical of big impression estimates and more interested in evidence they can verify: a GPS-tracked route, time-stamped photos from the street, and response they can count with QR codes, promo codes and call tracking. The strongest proof is the kind the client can check without taking anyone's word for it.
What to do: ask for the route and the photos as standard, and put a code on every screen.
5. Watching the campaign live
Clients increasingly expect to see their media running, not hear about it later. AOTC's Golden Ticket route room lets a client follow the truck on the map during the run, with photos from the street as they're taken, visible only to the brand that booked it.
What to do: ask your operator what you'll be able to see during the run, not just after it.
6. The truck as a venue
The same LED screens that advertise can host: watch parties, movie nights, brand activations and in-store events. Experiential and out-of-home budgets are blending, and a screen that can do both stretches each dollar further.
What to do: combine a route with an on-site session: advertise the event on the way, then park and become the screen. See LED screen truck rental .
7. Presence for causes and campaigns
Unions, causes and campaigns are using trucks to be physically present where decisions get made: outside a facility, alongside a march, on the streets of the wards that matter. Presence is hard to ignore, and it tends to end up in the news coverage.
What to do: plan routes around buildings and moments, not just audiences. See political and advocacy mobile billboards .
8. National reach, local routes
Brands launching in several cities want one partner, one plan and one standard, but they also want each city to feel local. The answer is national coordination with routes planned block by block in each market.
What to do: brief once, then insist on a city-specific route for every market. See AOTC's markets .
What it means for your next campaign
Plan from the calendar: find the moment first
Make creative that's worth filming
Build a creative system that changes by place and hour
Ask for a GPS-tracked route, photos and a way to count response
Ask what you'll see while it's running
Consider the screens as a venue, not just a billboard

### Best shareable OOH ad formats compared (https://adsofthecentury.net/shareable-ooh-ad-formats.html)
Key takeaways:
Shareability comes from surprise, place and timing more than from size alone.
3D anamorphic screens and stunts are the most viral but the most expensive and slowest to make.
Mobile LED trucks trade some spectacle for flexibility: right place, right hour, changeable message.
Murals and projections earn shares through craft and novelty in a specific location.
Whatever the format, design so the brand is legible in a phone photo.
The formats, side by side
Format Why people share it Commitment Flexibility
3D anamorphic screen The illusion of objects leaving the screen High: premium screens, costly CGI, weeks of production Low: one location
Stunt or installation Something physically unexpected High: build, permits, staffing Low once built
Projection Buildings turned into screens at night Medium: permission, equipment, crew Medium: night only
Hand-painted mural Craft, scale, local art Medium: wall rights, artist, days to paint Low: fixed message
Mobile LED truck The right message at the right place and hour Low to medium: hours or days High: changes by route and daypart
Vehicle wraps Bold design seen repeatedly Medium: printing and install Low: one design
Spectacle formats: big reach, big commitment
Anamorphic screens, installations and stunts produce the clips that travel furthest, but each takes significant budget, production time and approvals, and works in one place. They suit national brands with a single tentpole moment and a team ready to amplify it.
Craft formats: local and lasting
Murals and projections earn shares through artistry and novelty. A mural becomes a neighborhood landmark people photograph for months; a projection turns a building into a one-night event. Both need permission from building owners and, often, the city.
Moment formats: flexible and fast
A mobile LED truck doesn't need a special screen or a building. It goes where the crowd is, when it's there, with a message written for that moment: the game score, the festival set time, the launch countdown. That combination of place, timing and full-motion video is what makes people film it.
How to choose
One huge national moment, big budget: anamorphic screen or stunt, with a social plan behind it.
A neighborhood you want to own for months: a mural.
A night event or launch party: projection or a mobile LED truck on site.
Several moments across a city, or a tight timeline: mobile LED trucks.
Design rules that make any format shareable
Surprise first, message second
Tie it to the place or moment
Keep the brand legible in a vertical phone frame
Add a handle or hashtag people can tag
Film it yourself and post the best version
How AOTC makes moment formats shareable

### Chicago event advertising timeline guide for 2026 (https://adsofthecentury.net/chicago-event-advertising-timeline.html)
Key takeaways:
Start about 12 weeks out; the best street time around big Chicago weekends books early.
Check street closures and event-zone rules around the venue before routing.
Have creative final four weeks out so there's time for approvals and message changes.
On the day, time the route to gates opening and crowds letting out, not the middle of the event.
Measure with a code only the event ads use, and read results the week after.
1. Twelve weeks out: pick the moment and the goal
Decide which event you're riding and what you want from it: ticket sales, foot traffic to a nearby location, sponsor visibility or brand presence. Write the goal and how you'll measure it.
2. Eight weeks out: book the street media
Reserve the truck and any fixed screens for the days and hours you need. Around Chicago's biggest weekends, the best time slots go first, because every brand wants the same streets at the same hours.
3. Six weeks out: check closures and rules
Big events close streets and set perimeters, and the city may restrict vehicles near venues. Get the event's footprint and closure map, then plan routes on the approaches, transit stops and nearby districts instead. AOTC checks the city's rules for advertising vehicles before the truck rolls.
4. Four weeks out: finish the creative
Lock the loops for each screen, including versions for different dayparts (the morning teaser, the gates-open message, the after-party line). Leave time for client, sponsor or franchisor approvals.
5. Two weeks out: start the tease
Run social and email teasers aimed at the event's audience, and, if the goal is ticket sales, a first truck run through the neighborhoods where ticket buyers live.
6. Event week: run routes by daypart
Downtown commute and lunch routes reach office workers who are going that weekend. Evenings cover the nightlife districts where pre-parties happen. Change the message as the day gets closer.
7. Event day: time it to the crowd
Be on the approaches the hour before gates open and on the exits the hour after the crowd lets out. Those are the moments the most people are on the surrounding streets, moving slowly and looking around.
8. The week after: recap and measure
Pull code uses, ticket or sales data and brand search for the event days against the weeks before. Post the best photos from the run. Note which hours and corners worked for next year.
Chicago's big moments, late 2026 into 2027
Moment When Where the crowd is
Magnificent Mile Lights Festival The Saturday before Thanksgiving Michigan Avenue, River North
Holiday shopping and markets Late November through December State Street, Michigan Avenue, Daley Plaza
Chicago Auto Show February McCormick Place
Municipal election February 23, 2027 (runoffs April 6) All 50 wards
St. Patrick's weekend March The river downtown, the Loop, bars citywide
Cubs Opening Day Late March or April Wrigleyville
Sueños Memorial Day weekend Grant Park
Pride Late June Lakeview and Northalsted
Lollapalooza Late July or August Grant Park, the Loop, South Loop
Chicago Air and Water Show August North Avenue Beach, the lakefront
Chicago Marathon October 29 neighborhoods along the course
Dates move from year to year; confirm each event's official dates before booking. McCormick Place also hosts trade shows most of the year; see trade show mobile billboards .

### Chicago event promotion with mobile LED ads (https://adsofthecentury.net/chicago-event-promotion-mobile-led.html)
Key takeaways:
Use the screens before the event to sell tickets where buyers live and go out.
On the day, work the approaches, transit stops and nearby districts outside the closures.
Parked on site, an LED screen truck becomes the event's own screen: schedules, sponsors, live video.
Sponsor rotations on the screens add measurable value to partnership packages.
Route around the event's footprint; AOTC checks closures and vehicle rules before the truck rolls.
Five ways to use the screens
Use When Where Measure
Ticket push On-sale and the final 10 days Buyer neighborhoods, nightlife districts, downtown at lunch Ticket sales with a screen-only code
Day-of presence Gates opening, letting out Approaches, L stations, nearby blocks Walk-up sales, app opens
On-site screen During the event Parked inside or at the entrance Sponsor plays, schedule views
Sponsor rotation Throughout On the truck's loop Plays and photos for each sponsor
Recap The days after Buyer neighborhoods again Early sign-ups for next year
The ticket push
Pull ticket-buyer ZIP codes from past events and route the truck through those neighborhoods in the evenings during on-sale week and the final ten days. Downtown lunch routes reach office workers making weekend plans. Put the date, the headliner or the hook and a QR code to tickets on screen; nothing else.
Day-of presence
Most events close streets, so the truck works the approaches: the L stations that feed the gates, the main walking routes and the bar and restaurant blocks where people meet up first. On the screens: entrance directions, set times, the app and the sponsor of the hour.
The on-site screen
Parked on site, an LED screen truck turns into the event's own screen: schedules, wayfinding, sponsor ads, live video from the stage, even a movie night. It's booked by the hour or the event. See LED screen truck rental .
Sponsor value
Screen time is something you can add to a sponsorship package and document: the sponsor's ad in the loop, photos of it on the street and the GPS-tracked route showing where it ran.
The recap
The week after, run a thank-you and "save the date" through the buyer neighborhoods, and post the best photos from the run. Early-bird sign-ups for next year are the result to watch.
Routing around Chicago events
Get the event footprint and closure map early.
Plan staging spots outside the perimeter on the busiest approaches.
Expect traffic: build slack into the schedule on big days.
Have a rain plan; the screens work in weather, crowds move differently.

Eye-level screens reach pedestrians, drivers and riders at once, on both sides of the truck.
Downtown Chicago's crowds move on a schedule: commute, lunch, game time, nightlife.
Neighborhood corridors reach residents where they shop, eat and go out.
Book the truck in a rotation with up to six non-competing brands, or have it to yourself for the big moments.
Chicago is AOTC's home base, with campaigns across downtown and the neighborhoods.
Why street level works in Chicago
Chicago's downtown and its neighborhoods are dense, walkable and full of transit riders. Fixed billboards mostly line the expressways, well above the people walking the blocks. A mobile LED screen sits at eye level, faces both sidewalks at once and moves to where the crowd is, hour by hour.

### Chicago ward mobile LED campaigns (https://adsofthecentury.net/chicago-ward-mobile-led-campaigns.html)
Key takeaways:
Chicago votes for mayor, clerk, treasurer and all 50 aldermen on February 23, 2027; runoffs are April 6.
Ward races are won block by block, so routes should follow precincts, not the whole city.
Plan three phases: name recognition, early voting and get-out-the-vote, plus a runoff contingency.
Illinois requires political committees to identify themselves on their communications; confirm the wording with counsel.
Keep the truck outside the campaign-free zone around polling places on election day and at early-voting sites.
The 2027 election calendar
Date What happens
Winter 2026–27 Name-recognition and persuasion phase across the ward
Before election day Early voting and vote by mail; check the Chicago Board of Election Commissioners for exact dates and sites
February 23, 2027 Municipal election: mayor, clerk, treasurer and all 50 aldermen
April 6, 2027 Runoffs where no candidate won more than half the vote
Ward races are won block by block
An aldermanic race is local: a few tens of thousands of voters in one part of the city, with turnout that varies sharply by precinct. Citywide media wastes most of its reach outside the ward. A mobile LED screen can stay on the ward's commercial corridors, near its transit stops and on the blocks where the campaign needs turnout most.
Three phases, plus a runoff
Name recognition
Weeks before voting starts, run the candidate's name, the ward number and one clear reason, on the ward's busiest corridors at commute and weekend shopping hours.
Early voting
Once early voting opens, switch the message: where and when to vote early, routed past the corridors near early-voting sites (outside the campaign-free zone).
Get out the vote
In the final days, route through the precincts where turnout needs a push, at the hours people are home and out: evenings and the weekend before election day.
Runoff contingency
If the race goes to April 6, the same routes and creative adapt fast: new date, same name, the same blocks.
The rules
Disclosure. Illinois law requires political committees to identify themselves (a "paid for by" line) on their political communications. Confirm the exact wording with the campaign's counsel.
Campaign-free zones. Illinois bars electioneering within a set distance of polling place entrances. The truck stays outside those zones on election day and near early-voting sites.
Vehicle rules. AOTC checks the city's rules for advertising vehicles before the truck rolls.
Accuracy. Election dates and voting information must match the election authority's official information.
This guide isn't legal advice; the campaign's counsel has the final word.
On the screen
The candidate's name, as large as the screen allows
The ward number
One line: the reason or the issue
The phase message: "Vote early" or "Vote Feb. 23"
The required disclosure, legible
In multilingual wards, alternate languages within the loop.
How campaigns read the results
Volunteer and supporter sign-ups from a screen-only QR code
Name ID in the campaign's own polling, before and after
Early-vote turnout in targeted precincts vs. others
The GPS-tracked route, to match exposure with precinct results

Run every version past the dealership's compliance review before it airs

### Fraud-free local advertising in 2026 (https://adsofthecentury.net/fraud-free-local-advertising.html)
Key takeaways:
Estimates of digital ad fraud run to tens of billions of dollars a year; the World Federation of Advertisers put 2025 losses above $50 billion.
Fraud lives where software can fake the signal: clicks, impressions, app installs and form fills.
Out-of-home can't be loaded by a bot, so the risk shifts from fake impressions to how the audience is estimated.
Test every channel with one question: can I see it, or a record of it, for myself?
Pair street media with a QR code, promo code or call-tracking number so response is counted, not assumed.
Where local ad budgets leak
Ad fraud isn't only a big-brand problem. A local business buying search, social or programmatic display is exposed to the same tricks, just at a smaller scale. The World Federation of Advertisers estimated that fraud would cost advertisers more than $50 billion worldwide in 2025, and independent audits of paid clicks keep finding a meaningful share of traffic that isn't human. The common leaks:
Invalid clicks on search ads. Bots and competitors clicking your ads, each click billed.
Bot impressions on display and video. Ads "served" to software, or stacked where no person can see them.
Spoofed apps and devices. Inventory that claims to be a premium app or a TV screen and isn't.
Junk leads. Form fills from scripts that look like customers until someone calls them back.
Fake reach. Influencer audiences padded with purchased followers.
None of these show up as a line on the invoice. They show up as campaigns that "performed" on the dashboard and didn't move the register.
Which media can't be faked
The test is simple: can software produce the signal you're paying for? If it can, fraud is possible and you need verification. If it can't, the question becomes how well the audience is estimated.
Channel Can a bot fake it? What you can check
Search ads Clicks, yes Calls, bookings and sales tied to each click
Social ads Views and followers, yes Conversions, not likes
Programmatic display Impressions, yes Authorized-seller files (ads.txt), placement lists, conversions
Connected TV Spoofed apps and devices, yes Authorized sellers (app-ads.txt), direct buys
Fixed billboard No A photo of the board, its audited audience
Mobile LED billboard No GPS-tracked route, photos, live location
Direct mail No Postal receipts, response codes
The honest caveat: estimates aren't counts
A street screen can't be clicked by a bot, but nobody hands a counter to every person who walks past it either. Out-of-home audiences are estimated. That isn't fraud, but it is a number you should understand before you compare it with anything else.
AOTC estimates impressions conservatively: at least one viewer for every second the ad is on screen, plus the audited weekly audience of each billboard the route passes, credited only for the minutes the truck spends beside it. The number is labeled as an estimate for planning, not a guarantee, and the method is the same on every route.
A fraud-resistant local plan
Put the moment-driven money in the real world. The opening, the sale weekend, the event: show up where the customers physically are.
Keep digital spend tied to conversions. Pay for search and social only where you can see the calls, bookings or orders they produce.
Give every channel its own response code. One QR code, promo code or phone number per channel, so results don't blur together.
Ask every seller for the record. A photo, a route, a placement list. If there's no record, treat the number as a claim.
Compare against a baseline. Look at the same days the week or the year before, not at the campaign's own dashboard.
How AOTC keeps a campaign checkable
Every AOTC run comes with a GPS-tracked route and photos of the ad on the street, and clients can watch the truck live in the Golden Ticket route room while it drives. The record shows when your ad was in the rotation, so there's no question of whose ad was up.
To build response tracking into the plan from day one, start with how to plan a mobile billboard campaign , then see the complete guide to OOH sales attribution .

### Grand opening advertising for grocery stores in 2026 (https://adsofthecentury.net/grocery-store-grand-opening-advertising.html)
Key takeaways:
Grocery shoppers are creatures of habit; the opening has to give them a reason to change their route.
Draw the trade area by drive time and by the roads shoppers already use.
Run the most visible media on the days people shop: weekends and weekday evenings.
In-language creative tells a neighborhood the store was built for it.
Judge the opening by weeks two to six: repeat visits matter more than the opening-day line.
The real job: break a habit
Most households already have a grocery routine: the store on the way home, the weekly trip on Saturday morning, the app with saved coupons. A new store isn't competing for attention so much as for a place in that routine. The opening has to make the first visit easy and worth it, then make the second visit automatic.
Draw the trade area by drive time
Drive time, not distance. A store ten minutes away by a main road beats one five minutes away through side streets.
The roads shoppers use. Commute corridors, school routes and the approaches to current stores.
Walkers and transit riders in dense neighborhoods, who shop more often in smaller baskets.
Who lives there. Household size, languages spoken and the foods people look for.
Time it to the shopping week
When Who's shopping What to run
Weekday evenings Commuters on the way home Truck on the main commute corridors; "now open" plus the cross streets
Saturday morning Big weekly shops, families Truck around the trade area's busiest roads; the opening-week offer
Sunday Meal-prep and restock trips Social and digital coupons near parks and markets
Midweek mornings Older shoppers, quieter aisles Community outreach, senior hours, pharmacy messages
Give a reason to switch
Opening-week prices on staples people compare.
Digital coupons and a loyalty bonus for signing up in the first weeks.
A standout department: the bakery, the butcher, the hot food, the produce.
Local products from nearby makers, which also earns local press.
Convenience: parking, pickup, delivery, longer hours.
Speak the neighborhood's languages
In many trade areas, a large share of shoppers speak a language other than English at home. Running the opening message in those languages, on the screens and in print, tells the neighborhood the store was built for it. A digital screen can alternate languages within the same run.
What to measure
Loyalty and app sign-ups in opening week
Transactions and average basket in weeks one, two and six
Digital coupon redemptions by channel code
Repeat visits from the shoppers who signed up

No other grocer shares your rotation. For the basics of any opening, read key factors in promoting a new store opening , then see grand opening mobile billboards .

### How billboards amplify tech product launches (https://adsofthecentury.net/billboards-amplify-tech-launches.html)
Key takeaways:
Physical presence signals that a company is real and investing, which matters for new products.
Outdoor ads become social posts and press photos when they're placed and written to be shared.
The search lift from outdoor exposure is where most of the launch effect shows up online.
Launch-week timing matters more than months of presence for most tech products.
Mobile LED puts the message at the conference, the office district or the campus on the exact day.
1. The credibility signal
Anyone can buy a social ad. A product on a huge screen in the middle of a city reads differently: the company is real, it's investing, it expects to be around. For a new product, especially one asking people to trust it with data, money or their workflow, that signal does work a feed ad can't.
2. The ad becomes content
Outdoor ads that are clever, local or unexpected get photographed. A launch message on a full-motion screen in front of a crowd can travel far beyond the street it ran on, through employees, fans, journalists and people who just thought it was cool. That only happens on purpose: write for the photo, place it where people will see each other seeing it, and make the brand legible in a phone shot.
3. A hook for press
"Company X takes over the conference district" is a story; "Company X launches a feature" often isn't. A visible street presence gives reporters, analysts and creators a picture and an angle on launch day.
4. Search lift
Most people who notice a launch billboard don't scan anything. They remember the name and search for it later. That's why launch teams watch brand and product search volume, direct site traffic and app-store searches during launch week. It's also why search ads, the landing page and app-store listing must be ready before the first screen lights up.
Where to put launch screens
Launch audience Where they are
Developers and technical buyers Conference venues and hotels, tech districts, campuses
Business buyers Financial and office districts at commute and lunch
Consumers Shopping streets, nightlife, stadium and concert crowds
Press and investors Launch-event venue, conference press areas, downtown
Major tech moments cluster in a few cities, such as January's show week in Las Vegas , March festival season in Austin and the conference calendar in the San Francisco Bay Area and New York .
Why mobile LED fits launch week
Exact timing. The screen can be outside the keynote at 9 and in the after-party district at 9 p.m.
No long contract. Book the launch days, not four weeks.
Changeable message. "Tomorrow." Then "Live now." Then "Thanks, Austin."
No competitor in your rotation, and an exclusive booking if the launch needs the truck to itself.
How AOTC amplifies a launch
AOTC plans launch routes around the venues and districts where your audience is each hour, designs full-motion creative in-house, and sends a GPS-tracked route and photos after every run. The photos are useful for your own launch recap. For the full plan, read the complete guide to mobile LED tech launches , or see tech brand launch campaign ideas .

### How contractors stay visible between job cycles (https://adsofthecentury.net/contractor-visibility-between-jobs.html)
Key takeaways:
Visibility between jobs comes from a few always-on basics plus timed bursts, not constant spending.
Every finished job is advertising: yard signs, photos, reviews and the neighbors who watched.
Past customers are the cheapest next job; stay in touch on a schedule.
Short street-presence bursts in the neighborhoods you already serve keep the name familiar.
Track every lead's source so you know which basics and bursts fill the gaps.
The problem: work comes in waves
When the schedule is full, marketing stops because nobody has time. When the schedule empties, marketing starts in a hurry, and it takes weeks to produce calls. The fix is a small system that keeps running through both, so the next job is already on its way when the current one ends.
The always-on basics
The search listing. Complete, with service areas, hours and recent job photos.
Reviews. Ask every satisfied customer, every time, and answer every review.
Yard signs. At every job, where local rules and the customer allow.
Vehicles. Branded trucks and vans are seen in the same neighborhoods every day.
The website. Services, areas, photos and one clear way to book.
Every job is advertising
A finished kitchen, roof or driveway is the best ad a contractor has, and its audience is the neighbors who watched the work happen. While the sign is still in the yard, reach the rest of the street: door hangers, a post in the neighborhood group, and a short burst of street presence on the surrounding blocks.
Past customers: the cheapest next job
A check-in after the job, and again before the next relevant season
Maintenance reminders: filters, inspections, sealing, tune-ups
A referral offer for neighbors and friends
Bursts in the gaps
When Burst Where
A project wraps up Two or three days of street presence The blocks around the finished job
Before the busy season A week of screens and social The neighborhoods that hire you most
A quiet stretch in the schedule A few days with an offer for booking now Your best-performing ZIP codes
A community event The truck at the festival or game Where neighbors gather
A mobile LED billboard suits these bursts because it can cover specific neighborhoods for just a few days, at the hours homeowners are out.
Track where the work comes from
Ask every caller how they heard of you, use a separate phone number or link for paid bursts, and log the source with every booked job. After a few cycles you'll know which basics and which bursts fill the gaps.
How AOTC helps contractors stay visible

No competing contractor shares your rotation. For lead generation specifically, read mobile LED ads for contractor lead generation ; for timing, seasonal outdoor advertising for home services .

### How franchisees drive opening-week traffic (https://adsofthecentury.net/franchise-opening-week-traffic.html)
Key takeaways:
Opening week works best as a sequence, not a single day: tease, open, push, follow up.
Use the soft opening to fix operations before the crowd arrives.
Put the most visible media on opening day and the first weekend, routed by daypart.
Collect a way to reach every first-time customer: app, loyalty or text sign-up.
Plan the week-two offer before opening day so first visits turn into habits.
1. Seven days out: announce the date everywhere
Put the opening date on the building, the local listings, social and email, and run a teaser on the mobile LED screens along the commute and lunch routes: the brand, "Opening Friday" and the street name. The goal is that anyone who passes the trade area that week knows the day.
2. Three days out: invite the neighbors
Drop invitations and first-week offers at nearby offices, schools, gyms and shops. Ask the chamber of commerce and local officials to the ribbon cutting. Invite local press and creators to the soft opening.
3. One day out: run the soft opening
An invite-only or friends-and-family service trains the team on real orders, finds the slow spots in the line and gives local creators something to post. Fix what breaks before the public arrives.
4. Opening day: make it impossible to miss
Route the mobile LED billboard by daypart: commuters in the morning, offices and schools at lunch, neighborhoods at dinner, parking or circling near the site where it's allowed. Keep the message to the brand, "Now open", the street and one offer. Staff the doors with a QR code for app, loyalty or text sign-up.
5. The first weekend: push for new faces
Weekends reach the people who missed opening day: families, shoppers and weekend errands. Run the truck on the busiest weekend corridors near the site, and post the opening-day crowd on social with the weekend offer.
6. Days six and seven: talk to everyone you met
Send the first follow-up to every sign-up: thanks for coming, and a reason to return in week two. Answer every new review. Note which hours were busy and which were slow.
7. Week two: turn first visits into habits
Bring the screens back for the hours that were slow, with a message aimed at regulars, such as the lunch special for offices or a family night. Compare week-two transactions with opening week to see whether the opening built a base.
Where the opening budget goes
Tactic When Why
Mobile LED billboard Teaser day, opening day, first weekend Everyone in the trade area sees it, at full size
Social in the trade area The week before through week two Repeats the date and the offer
Local listings and reviews Before opening and every day after Catches the searches the street creates
Sign-up offer Opening week Gives you a way back to every first-time guest
How AOTC runs opening week
AOTC plans the teaser and opening routes around your trade area, designs creative to your brand's standards, and sends a GPS-tracked route and photos after every run. No competing brand shares your rotation, and an exclusive booking gives you the truck to yourself for opening day. ### How to add OOH to a digital media plan in 2026 (https://adsofthecentury.net/add-ooh-to-digital-media-plan.html)
Key takeaways:
OOH's job in a digital plan is reach in the real world: people who skip, block or scroll past ads.
Start with a test you can measure, then shift budget based on results.
Translate audience segments into places and hours: where is this person at 8 a.m., noon and 9 p.m.?
One creative idea across channels makes each exposure reinforce the others.
Watch brand search and direct traffic in the exposed areas: that's where OOH shows up first.
1. Give OOH one job
In a digital plan, out-of-home usually does what feeds can't: put the brand in front of everyone in a place, at a moment, with no skip button. Decide whether that job is awareness in a new market, traffic to a location, presence at an event, or a launch people talk about.
One clear job makes every later choice (format, area, creative, measurement) easier.
2. Fund it as a measurable test
Move a slice of budget that's big enough to own one area or moment, and keep the rest of the plan steady while it runs. A focused, readable test beats a token amount spread too thin to show up in the numbers.
3. Map digital audiences to places and hours
Take your best-performing segments and ask where those people physically are during the day. Office workers: the business district at commute and lunch. Students: campus and nightlife. Families: shopping centers and youth sports on weekends. That map becomes the OOH plan.
4. Use one creative idea everywhere
The screen on the street and the ad in the feed should look like the same campaign: same line, same colors, same visual. Outdoor makes the idea big; digital repeats it and adds the click. On a moving screen keep it to one message and a name people can search.
5. Sequence street first, digital second
Run OOH in an area, then follow with social, CTV or search in the same ZIP codes during the same days. People who saw the truck at lunch see the brand again on their phone that evening, and the second exposure lands harder.
6. Give OOH its own response path
A QR code, short URL, promo code or call-tracking number that appears only on the out-of-home screens. It won't capture everyone, but it gives you an exact floor to set beside the broader lift.
7. Read lift, then reallocate
Compare brand searches, direct site visits, calls and sales in the exposed areas against the weeks before and against a similar area that didn't get the campaign. If cost per response holds up against your digital channels, scale it; if not, change one thing (area, daypart, message) and test again.
What each channel does in the combined plan
Channel Job Signal to watch
Mobile LED / DOOH Reach in a place and moment Brand search, direct traffic, code uses
Social Repeat the idea, drive clicks Clicks, conversions in the same areas
CTV Reach households at home Site visits and search after airings
Search Catch the demand OOH creates Brand-term volume and conversions
How AOTC fits into a digital plan
AOTC plans the street side: routes by daypart, creative made for the truck's screens, a GPS-tracked route and photos after every run, and estimated impressions you can set beside digital numbers. Standard bookings rotate up to six brands, with no competitor in your rotation. To see a design on the truck first, try the free Display Studio . For the concepts behind this, read understanding OOH in a digital media plan .

### How to measure OOH sales lift with GPS route data (https://adsofthecentury.net/measure-ooh-sales-lift-gps.html)
Key takeaways:
Decide the metric and the baseline before the campaign starts, not after.
Use a control area the route never enters, as similar to the test area as you can find.
The GPS-tracked route with times is what lets you match sales to the hours and streets the ad actually ran.
Calculate lift against both areas' own baselines so seasonality cancels out.
Treat response codes as the floor and the matched-area lift as the estimate.
1. Pick one sales metric and a baseline
Choose the number the campaign should move, such as transactions, revenue, new customers, calls or bookings, and the period you'll compare it with, usually the same weeks before the campaign and, if you have it, the same weeks last year.
Write both down before the truck rolls. Choosing the metric after you've seen the results is how campaigns end up "working" on paper.
2. Choose a test area and a control area
Pick two areas that behave alike: similar neighborhoods, similar store sales, similar seasonality. The campaign runs in the test area only. The control area gets nothing new, so it shows you what would have happened anyway.
If you have several locations, pair them up: each store in the test group gets a similar partner in the control group.
3. Plan the route inside the test area
Route the truck by daypart through the streets that feed the test locations, and keep it out of the control area entirely, including the drive to and from the route. A control area the truck crossed on the way to lunch is no longer a control.
4. Collect the GPS-tracked route with times
The route record shows where the vehicle was at every point of the run. It answers the questions a sales analysis needs: which blocks, which hours, how long beside each location.
AOTC sends the GPS-tracked route and photos of the ad on the street after every run. During the run, the Golden Ticket route room shows the truck live.
5. Line up your sales with the route
Put sales by day and hour next to the route's times for each location in both groups. A simple sheet works: one row per location per day, with the hours the truck was nearby, sales and calls.
Column Where it comes from
Location and group Your list: test or control
Date and hours exposed The GPS-tracked route
Sales, transactions, calls Your point of sale and phone system
Code uses Your QR, promo code or call-tracking reports
Notes Weather, local events, promotions
6. Add a response code for an exact floor
Put one QR code, promo code or call-tracking number on the screens and nowhere else. Its count is exact but incomplete, because many people act without using it. It gives you a minimum to set beside the lift estimate.
7. Calculate the lift
Compare each group with its own baseline, then compare the groups: lift = (test after ÷ test before) ÷ (control after ÷ control before) − 1.
Example, for illustration only: if test-area sales rise from 1,000 to 1,150 transactions (up 15%) while the control rises from 1,000 to 1,030 (up 3%), lift is 1.15 ÷ 1.03 − 1, or about 11.7%. That 11.7% is the estimated extra business the campaign drove in the test area.
8. Repeat, then change one thing
One test is a reading, two are a pattern. Run the next flight with one change, such as a different daypart, message or neighborhood, and compare again. Over a few flights you learn which hours and streets pay back.
How AOTC helps set up the test
We plan the route around your test locations, keep the vehicle out of the control areas, and send the GPS-tracked route, photos and estimated impressions after every run. For the cleanest read, book the test exclusively so the truck carries only your brand in the test area. For the bigger picture, see the complete guide to OOH sales attribution and geographic targeting for local campaigns .

### Key event promotion factors for Chicago venues (https://adsofthecentury.net/chicago-venue-event-promotion.html)
Key takeaways:
Promote where ticket buyers live and go out, not only around the venue itself.
The L shapes who can get to a show; promote along the lines that serve your doors.
Check the city calendar: a big game or festival the same night changes everything.
Most promotion budgets work hardest at on-sale and in the final week.
Partner with nearby bars and restaurants; the pre-show crowd is a shared audience.
The factors at a glance
Factor Ask Where street media helps
Neighborhood draw Where do our buyers live and go out? Routes through those neighborhoods at night and on weekends
Transit Which L lines and buses reach our doors? Stations and corridors along those lines
Competing nights What else is on: a game, a festival, another show? Timing the push around the conflict
Ticket timeline When do people buy: on-sale or last week? Bursts at on-sale and in the final days
Arrival and exit When is the street full around us? The hour before doors and after the show
Weather How does the season change behavior? Messages and hours that fit the season
Partners Who else benefits from our crowd? Shared screens with nearby bars and restaurants
Neighborhood draw
A venue's audience rarely lives next door. Look at ticket-buyer ZIP codes: an Uptown music hall may sell heavily to the North Side lakefront, while a West Loop room draws from across the city. Promote where buyers are, especially on the nights they go out.
Transit
The L decides who can get home easily after a show. Promote along the lines that serve your doors (the Red Line for Wrigleyville and Uptown, the Blue Line for Wicker Park and the West Loop corridor, the Brown Line for the North Side's neighborhood venues) and mention the nearest stop on screen.
Competing nights
A Cubs game, a Bears Sunday, a big festival or a United Center concert can fill or empty your street. Check the calendar before setting promotion dates. On a competing night, a screen near the big event's exits can still sell your late show or next date.
The ticket timeline
Announcement: social and email to your list; a first screen run in the buyers' neighborhoods.
On-sale: urgency on every channel; "On sale now" on the screens.
The middle weeks: lighter presence; social retargeting.
The final 7 to 10 days: the biggest push; routes through buyer neighborhoods every evening.
Show night: the screen outside the venue for walk-ups and the next date.
Weather and the season
Chicago's winters shorten time outdoors and push decisions later; summers fill patios and sidewalks and favor walk-ups. Adjust hours and messages: "Warm inside, two minutes from the Red Line" in January, "Patio open before the show" in July.
Partners
The bars and restaurants on your block share your crowd. Split screen time or run a joint message: dinner before, the show after. It extends the budget and gives the audience a plan for the night.

Standard bookings are rotational, with no competing venue in your rotation. Next: Chicago event promotion with mobile LED ads and the Chicago event advertising timeline .

### Key factors in promoting a new store opening (https://adsofthecentury.net/new-store-opening-promotion.html)
Key takeaways:
Draw the trade area from where people actually travel, not a circle on a map.
Pick an opening date that doesn't compete with a big local event, or one that rides it on purpose.
Visibility beats cleverness: people need to know the name, the street and the day.
A store that isn't staffed and stocked for the crowd turns opening buzz into bad reviews.
Plan the follow-up and the measurement before opening day, not after.
The ten factors at a glance
Factor The question to ask The common mistake
Trade area Where will customers come from, and how do they travel? Drawing a neat circle that ignores highways and habits
Timing What else is happening that week? Opening against a festival that blocks the streets
Visibility Can people see the store and find the entrance? Assuming the sign alone will do it
The offer What makes today worth a trip? An offer too complicated to remember
Readiness Can staff and stock handle a crowd? Buzz that ends in long lines and empty shelves
Community Who nearby should hear first? Skipping neighbors, schools and the chamber
Media mix What reaches the trade area at the right hours? Spreading the budget too thin for too long
Permits What do signs, events and vehicles need locally? Finding out the day before
Follow-up How will first visitors come back? No sign-up, no second offer
Measurement How will you know what worked? One promo code shared across every channel
Trade area: where the crowd comes from
Start with the paths people already travel: the commute that passes the site, the shopping trips to nearby anchors, the school runs and lunch breaks. Those paths, not a radius, decide where your opening media should run.
Timing: the day and the calendar
A late-week opening puts the first weekend right behind it. Check the local calendar for games, festivals, parades and holidays. Sometimes a big event is a gift, with crowds on your street. Sometimes it closes the roads. Decide which before you pick the date.
Visibility: name, street, day
People need three facts: who you are, where you are and when you open. Every piece of opening media should carry all three, in that order. A mobile LED billboard on the trade area's busiest streets is one of the most direct ways to put those three facts in front of everyone, at full size, in the days that matter.
The media mix that works
Before: signage on the building, listings and maps, social in the trade area, a teaser run on the screens.
Opening day: the truck routed by daypart around the site, the doors staffed with a sign-up QR code, local press invited.
First weekend: the truck on weekend shopping corridors, social showing the opening crowd.
Week two: a follow-up offer to every sign-up and a second run for the slow hours.
Permits and rules
Banners, sidewalk signs, inflatables, live music and advertising vehicles can each fall under local rules. Ask the city early. AOTC checks each city's rules for advertising vehicles before the truck rolls.
How to measure the opening
Opening-week transactions and new-customer counts
Sign-ups from the opening QR code
Offer redemptions by channel, each with its own code
Week-two and week-four sales: did the opening build regulars?
How AOTC promotes store openings

On a standard booking, every screen shows your store alone. ### Local DOOH media planning guide for 2026 (https://adsofthecentury.net/local-dooh-media-planning-guide.html)
Key takeaways:
Start from where your customers actually live and work, not from a radius on a map.
Each DOOH format does a different job; pick by goal, not by price alone.
Short flights around moments usually beat thin coverage spread over a month.
Design for two or three seconds: one message, big type, a clear name.
Decide how you'll measure before you buy: codes, calls and a baseline.
1. Draw the trade area from real customers
Pull the ZIP codes or addresses of your recent customers and map them. The shape you get, not a neat circle, is your trade area. Add the places those customers spend their day: the commute corridor, the office district, the stadium, the shopping street.
2. Match the format to the goal
Each kind of screen does a different job. Pick the ones that fit what you need to happen.
Format Best for Typical buy
Fixed digital billboard Always-on presence on one road Weeks, or programmatic by the impression
Place-based screens A specific audience: gyms, bars, offices, stores By venue network or impression
Mobile LED billboard truck Openings, events, game days, neighborhoods Hours or days, route planned by daypart
3. Set a test-sized budget
Put enough behind one flight to be noticed in one area, rather than a little everywhere. A focused test you can measure is worth more than a broad buy you can't read. Keep the rest of your marketing steady during the test so the result is clear.
4. Flight it by daypart and moment
Schedule screens for the hours your audience is actually out: commuters in the morning, office workers at lunch, diners and nightlife after dark, crowds before and after events. Around a big moment, such as an opening or a game, concentrate the budget into the days that matter.
5. Design for a few seconds
People read outdoor screens in two or three seconds, often while moving. One message, five to seven words, your name large, high contrast, and one clear action such as a short URL or a QR code big enough to scan from a sidewalk. Use the screen's motion to draw the eye, not to tell a long story.
6. Plan the measurement before you buy
Give the DOOH campaign its own QR code, promo code or phone number, and compare sales, calls and brand searches with the weeks before. If you have several locations, keep one similar area without the campaign as a control.
The local DOOH checklist
Trade area mapped from real customers
Formats chosen by goal
Dates and dayparts set around moments
Creative sized for each screen and readable in seconds
A response code used only on DOOH
A baseline period and, if possible, a control area

Clients see the truck live in the Golden Ticket route room.
