### Mobile billboard CPM vs. CTV and social ads (https://adsofthecentury.net/mobile-billboard-cpm-vs-ctv-social.html)
Key takeaways:
CPM = cost ÷ impressions × 1,000; it's the starting point for comparison, not the answer.
AOTC mobile LED campaigns benchmark at about $4 to $7 CPM on estimated impressions.
Published 2026 CTV benchmarks cluster around $25 to $35 CPM; social video is commonly $10 to $30.
Street impressions are estimated; digital impressions are counted but can include bots and spoofed devices.
Compare on cost per response too: use a separate code or number for each channel.
The numbers, side by side
Channel Typical CPM How impressions are counted Can it be skipped?
Mobile LED billboard (AOTC) About $4 to $7 Estimated from the route: at least one viewer per second on screen, plus the audiences of the billboards it passes No
Connected TV About $25 to $35 for most buys (published 2026 benchmarks) Counted by the ad server, per household Usually not, but often on a second screen
Social video About $10 to $30 Counted by the platform; a view can be a second or two Yes, by scrolling
CTV and social prices move with targeting, season and inventory, and premium placements cost more. Treat the ranges as orientation, then compare real quotes.
How to work out a CPM
CPM = cost ÷ impressions × 1,000. For illustration: an evening route that costs $1,500 and delivers an estimated 250,000 impression opportunities works out to a $6 CPM. A CTV flight that costs $1,500 at a $30 CPM buys 50,000 household impressions.
What an impression means in each
On the street, an impression is a person with a real chance to see a large, bright screen at eye level. Nobody can skip it, block it or scroll past it, but it isn't counted one person at a time, so it's estimated.
On CTV, an impression is an ad delivered to a TV in a household. It's usually watched through, but the room may be empty or the viewer on a phone, and spoofed devices are a known risk.
On social, an impression can be a fraction of a second in a fast-moving feed. Platforms count it precisely, but attention varies hugely.
How to compare fairly
Start with CPM to see what reach costs.
Adjust for attention. A skippable or second-screen impression isn't worth the same as an unskippable one.
Adjust for waste. Digital counts may include invalid traffic; street counts are estimates. Ask about both.
Finish with cost per response. Give each channel its own QR code, promo code or phone number, then divide spend by responses.
When each one wins
Goal Strongest channel
Own a neighborhood, venue or event for a day Mobile LED billboard
Reach households across a metro at home CTV
Drive clicks and retarget Social
Get filmed and shared Mobile LED billboard, then social
How AOTC quotes a CPM
Every AOTC quote can include an estimated impression count for the planned route, worked out with the same method we use in the Golden Ticket route room afterward, so you can set the truck beside your CTV and social numbers before you book. Standard bookings are rotational, which keeps the CPM low; exclusive bookings are quoted separately. Read the cost questions in the FAQ , see the launch-specific comparison in mobile billboards vs. CTV vs. social for tech launches , or text (773) 708-1400 for a route and a number.

### Mobile billboards vs CTV vs social for tech launches (https://adsofthecentury.net/tech-launch-mobile-billboard-vs-ctv-social.html)
Key takeaways:
Mobile billboards own a place and a day; CTV owns the living room; social owns the click.
AOTC mobile LED campaigns benchmark at about $4 to $7 CPM on estimated impressions; published 2026 CTV benchmarks cluster around $25 to $35.
B2B launches lean on mobile billboards at conferences plus targeted social.
Consumer app launches lean on social and CTV, with street presence in key cities for shareable moments.
Whatever the mix, have search ads and the landing page ready before launch day.
Side by side
Mobile billboard CTV Social
Best at Owning a place and a day Household reach, storytelling Targeting, clicks, retargeting
Targeting Streets, venues and hours Households by data segment People by interest, role, behavior
Shareability High: people film the screen Low Native, but crowded
Skippable? No Usually not, but often a second screen Yes, by scrolling
Typical CPM About $4 to $7 (AOTC benchmark, estimated impressions) About $25 to $35 for most buys About $10 to $30 for video
Creative needed Short loops sized for each screen A 15- or 30-second spot Many short variants
Measurement QR code, search lift, GPS route, photos Site visits and search after airings Clicks and conversions
B2B software launches
Buyers are a narrow group gathered in predictable places: the conference, the financial district, a few office parks. A mobile billboard outside the venue during show week reaches them in person, at a fraction of the cost of broad media, and gives the sales team something to talk about. Pair it with targeted social on professional platforms and search on the product name.
Consumer app launches
Reach matters more, and the audience is everywhere. Social and CTV carry the volume. Street presence in two or three key cities creates the moments that social can amplify: the screen people film, the QR code that drives first downloads, the launch-day photo for press.
Hardware and devices
People want to see the thing. Full-motion LED screens can show the product at a scale a phone can't, outside retailers that stock it or at launch events. CTV tells the longer story at home; social drives preorders.
Suggested mixes
Launch type Lead channel Support
B2B software at a conference Mobile billboard at the venue Targeted social, search
Consumer app Social and CTV Mobile billboard in key cities, search
Hardware or device CTV and mobile LED near retailers and events Social for preorders, search
Local tech or startup Mobile billboard in the home city Social in the same ZIP codes
Measuring the mix
Give each channel its own code or link, then read the launch as a whole: total sign-ups or downloads, brand and product search volume, and direct traffic from the launch cities against the weeks before. Street exposure often shows up as search and direct traffic rather than as its own clicks.

### Mobile LED ads built for social sharing (https://adsofthecentury.net/social-shareable-mobile-led-ads.html)
Key takeaways:
Place comes first: run the ad where people already have their phones out.
A reason to film beats a reason to read: reveal, joke, local reference.
Phones crop landscape screens; keep the brand in the middle third of the side screen.
Seed the first posts with your own team or creators, then repost fans' clips.
Count mentions, tags, views and QR scans, not just street impressions.
1. Run it where phones are already out
Crowds at games, concerts, festivals, parades, launch events and nightlife districts are already filming. Put the truck there at the moment the crowd is thickest: gates opening, the final out, the set ending, last call.
2. Give people a reason to film
A reveal, a countdown, a joke about the moment, a reference to the exact street or team. Something a person would show a friend. An ad that's only information gets read; an ad that's a moment gets filmed.
3. Frame it for a vertical phone shot
Most people film in portrait, which crops the wide side screen. Keep the brand and the punchline in the middle third, large enough to read in a quick clip. Use high contrast: LED glows on camera, but thin type and pale colors wash out.
4. Use motion that rewards waiting
Build the loop so the payoff comes a few seconds in, after a setup. People keep filming to catch the reveal, and the clip has a beginning, middle and end. Keep each loop short so a passerby sees the whole thing.
5. Add a handle or hashtag
Put your social handle or a short hashtag on screen so posts can tag you and you can find them. One, not three.
6. Seed the first posts
Have your own team, ambassadors or a few creators film and post in the first hour. Early posts make the moment discoverable and show others it's worth sharing.
7. Capture and repost the best clips
Search your handle, hashtag and location tags during and after the run. Repost the best fan clips (with permission) and use AOTC's run photos for your own recap.
8. Measure the social reach
Count tags, mentions, views of the clips, follower growth during the run and QR scans from the screens, alongside brand search in the city that day.
The screens, for design
Screen Pixels Role in a shareable ad
Each side (11.76 × 6.30 ft) 1920 × 1029 The moment: the reveal or the joke, brand centered
Rear (6.71 × 6.30 ft) 1080 × 1014 Close to a phone's shape; great for the handle and QR code
Front (6.71 × 3.36 ft) 1280 × 641 A short brand line

### Mobile LED ads for contractor lead generation (https://adsofthecentury.net/contractor-lead-generation-led-ads.html)
Key takeaways:
Route the truck where your most profitable jobs come from, not across the whole metro.
Time it to the season or a trigger moment, when homeowners are already thinking about the work.
The screen's job is a phone call: company, service, number, one offer.
Answer the phone live during the run; leads cool quickly.
A screen-only phone number and a 'how did you hear about us?' question make the results clear.
1. Pick the neighborhoods your best jobs come from
Pull the addresses of your most profitable recent jobs and look for the clusters: the subdivisions with older roofs, the blocks of homes due for new HVAC, the areas where remodels pay well. Those clusters are the route.
2. Time the run to the season or a trigger
Run when homeowners are already thinking about the work: before and during your trade's peak season, and right after trigger moments like a hailstorm, the first freeze or the first heat wave. See seasonal outdoor advertising for home services for the calendar.
3. Design for a phone call
Company name, the service in a few words, and a phone number big enough to read from across the street. "Roof damage? Free inspection." Show a real photo of your work if it reads at a glance. Hold the number on screen long enough to remember.
4. Add one booking offer
One reason to call now: a free inspection, a tune-up price, a discount for booking this month. One offer, not three.
5. Include the license and credentials
Some trades and states require a license number in advertising. Add it, along with what builds trust at a glance: "Licensed and insured," "Family owned since," years in business or the neighborhoods you serve.
6. Have the follow-up ready
Someone should answer the phone live while the truck is running. The landing page the QR code opens should load fast on a phone and offer a simple booking form. Leads that wait a day often book someone else.
7. Track every lead
Use a call-tracking number only the screens show, ask every caller how they heard of you, and log the source with every booked job. Compare calls from the routed neighborhoods with the weeks before; the GPS-tracked route shows where and when the ad ran.
Sample routes by trade
Trade Where When
Roofing and siding Older subdivisions; storm-hit areas Spring, fall and after storms
HVAC Neighborhoods of homes 10 to 20 years old Before the first heat wave and the first freeze
Remodeling Established neighborhoods, home-improvement store traffic Late winter and spring planning season
Landscaping Single-family neighborhoods, weekend errands Early spring
Plumbing Older housing stock, dense neighborhoods The first hard freeze; spring thaw

### Mobile LED ads for personal injury law firms (https://adsofthecentury.net/personal-injury-mobile-led-ads.html)
Key takeaways:
Aim for recall in specific communities, measured over weeks, not instant calls.
Route along commuter corridors, industrial areas at shift change and neighborhood shopping streets.
Firm name, practice area, an easy number or short URL: nothing else on screen.
Clear every version with ethics counsel; keep placement away from accident scenes and hospitals.
Run in repeated bursts and track calls with a screen-only number.
1. Set a recall goal for specific communities
Decide which communities the firm wants to be known in, and what people there should remember: the firm's name, the practice area and how to reach it. Personal injury needs are unpredictable, so the goal is to be the name people think of when they need one.
2. Choose routes and hours
Map where people in those communities spend their day, then route the truck there at the right hours.
Where When Who
Commuter corridors Morning and evening rush Drivers and transit riders
Industrial and logistics areas Shift changes Workers in physically demanding jobs
Neighborhood shopping streets Weekend afternoons Families and residents
Community events Festivals, parades, games Neighbors in one place
Keep the truck away from accident scenes, emergency rooms, hospitals and funerals.
3. Design for recall
Five to seven words plus the firm name and an easy number or short URL. "Hurt at work? Call [Firm]." Match the colors and look of the firm's other ads so every exposure builds the same memory. Hold the number on screen long enough to read twice.
4. Clear compliance before anything runs
Have ethics counsel check every version against the state's rules of professional conduct: truthful and not misleading, a responsible lawyer or firm identified, and any state-specific labels or limits on testimonials and past results. Include translated versions.
5. Run it in repeated bursts
Recall comes from repetition. Book a few days at a time on the same corridors each month rather than a single day once, and keep the message consistent across bursts.
6. Track calls and judge by signed cases
Show a call-tracking number used nowhere else, ask every caller where they heard of the firm, and compare call volume from the areas the truck drove against the weeks before. The GPS-tracked route shows exactly where and when the ad ran. Judge the channel by signed cases per dollar.
Campaign checklist
Communities and recall goal defined
Routes by hour, away from sensitive locations
Creative in every needed language
Compliance sign-off on every version
Screen-only call-tracking number live
Intake asks "where did you hear about us?"

### Mobile LED advertising for real estate listings (https://adsofthecentury.net/real-estate-listing-led-advertising.html)
Key takeaways:
Open houses are the strongest use: the truck routes traffic to the door in the hours before and during.
A full-motion screen shows a luxury listing's photos and video at a size that stops people.
Repeated presence in one neighborhood builds an agent's name for future listings.
Showing sellers a street-level launch plan can help win the listing appointment.
Include the brokerage name and follow fair-housing rules on every screen.
Five uses for agents and brokerages
Use On the screen When
Open-house traffic "Open house today, 1–4," the address, a photo The hours before and during
Listing launch Photos or a video tour, "Just listed," a QR code The first weekend on the market
Neighborhood farming The agent, the neighborhood, recent sales Repeated days each month
Listing appointments Part of the marketing plan shown to sellers Before the appointment
Recruiting The brokerage's pitch to agents Near real estate offices, at industry events
Open houses: the strongest use
Most open-house visitors come from the neighborhood and the main roads into it. Route the truck along those roads in the two hours before the open house and the first hour of it, with the address, the time and an arrow-simple direction. Park or circle nearby during the event where it's allowed. Count sign-ins against the brokerage's usual open-house traffic.
Luxury and standout listings
A full-motion LED screen can show a listing's best photos and video at a size no yard sign can. For a luxury home or a unique property, a launch weekend on the routes of likely buyers, and through the neighborhood itself, makes the listing an event, and the photos of it make good marketing for the agent too.
Farming a neighborhood
Agents build listings by being the familiar name in a neighborhood. A few days a month on the same streets, with the agent's face, the neighborhood name and recent results, keeps the name in front of future sellers between mailers and door knocks.
The rules on every screen
Brokerage name. State license laws, Illinois's included, generally require licensees' ads to include the sponsoring brokerage's name.
Fair housing. No wording or imagery that states or implies a preference or limitation based on protected characteristics.
Accuracy. Prices, features and "sold" claims must be current and true.
Seller consent. Get the seller's approval before featuring their home and address.
Your managing broker has the final word on compliance.
Creative that works
One great photo or a short video loop
"Open today 1–4" or "Just listed," and the street
A QR code to the listing page, large enough to scan
The agent and brokerage name
How AOTC works with agents
AOTC has run real estate campaigns in downtown Chicago. We route the truck around open houses and launches at the right hours, design the screens in-house for your broker's review and send a GPS-tracked route and photos after every run, which are useful to show sellers. ### Mobile LED DOOH campaigns for 2026 growth (https://adsofthecentury.net/mobile-led-dooh-growth-campaigns.html)
Key takeaways:
Growth campaigns aim at people who don't know you yet, so reach in the right place matters more than frequency.
Mobile LED fits five growth jobs: launches, market entry, seasonal peaks, event surround and neighborhood presence.
Bursts around moments usually outperform the same budget spread evenly across a month.
Measure every flight the same way so you can compare and scale the winners.
Scale by repeating a proven route pattern in new neighborhoods or new cities.
Why mobile LED suits growth
Growth means reaching people who haven't chosen you yet. Online, that's expensive: you're bidding against every competitor for the same audience in the same feed. On the street, a moving LED screen reaches everyone on the route, including people who never would have clicked, and it can be in the exact neighborhood, venue or event where new customers are concentrated.
Five growth campaign types
Type The job Typical flight Measure
Launch Make a new product, store or service feel big 1 to 7 days Brand search, launch-day sales, social mentions
Market entry Introduce the brand in a new city or neighborhood Bursts over 2 to 8 weeks New customers from the new area
Seasonal peak Win the weeks when the category is bought The peak days of the season Sales vs. last season
Event surround Own the streets around a game, festival or show Event days, before and after Code uses, visits during the event
Neighborhood presence Become the familiar name in a trade area Recurring days each month Repeat visits, calls, reviews
Bursts beat even spreading
A truck that dominates the right streets for a few days is noticed and remembered. The same budget spread across a month can disappear into the background. Plan in bursts around moments (the opening weekend, the first warm Saturday, the big game) and leave gaps between them rather than running thin every day.
Creative that grows the audience
Say who you are first. New audiences need the name and what you do before anything else.
Use motion to stop people. A reveal, a countdown or a bold animation turns heads; keep the message itself short.
Localize. Naming the neighborhood or the event tells people the ad is for them.
Change by daypart. Morning, lunch and evening crowds respond to different offers.
Give one next step. A short URL, a QR code big enough to scan, or "now open on Main Street."
From one flight to a growth plan
Run a first flight in one area with one response code and a baseline.
Keep the winners: the dayparts, streets and messages that produced the response.
Repeat the pattern in a similar neighborhood, then compare.
Add markets once the pattern holds, using a tour or multi-market plan .
Fill the gaps between bursts with a rotational booking, sharing the truck with non-competing brands.
How AOTC runs growth campaigns
AOTC plans every route by daypart around the audience, designs creative in-house for the truck's two side screens, rear and front, and sends a GPS-tracked route and photos after every run. No competing brand shares your rotation, and you can watch the truck live in the Golden Ticket route room. For the market context read what's driving DOOH growth in 2026 , then text (773) 708-1400 with the city and dates.

### Mobile LED DOOH for omnichannel media plans (https://adsofthecentury.net/mobile-led-dooh-omnichannel.html)
Key takeaways:
Mobile LED is the touchpoint people meet in the real world; digital channels follow it up.
Surround, tease-and-reveal and event surround are the three proven sequencing patterns.
Match the areas and days: digital follow-up should target the same ZIP codes the truck drove.
One creative idea across every channel makes each exposure reinforce the last.
Give each channel its own code, then read lift across the plan instead of channel by channel.
The part mobile LED plays
Every channel in an omnichannel plan has a job. Search catches demand. Social repeats the idea and takes the click. CTV reaches households at home. Email talks to people who already know you. Mobile LED is the one channel people meet in the real world, at full size, in their own neighborhood, which is why the others work better after it.
Three sequencing patterns
Surround
The truck drives a neighborhood at lunch and dinner. The same days, social and CTV run in the same ZIP codes and search ads are ready for the brand terms. People see the brand on the street, then again on their phone that evening.
Tease and reveal
The screens tease ("Something's coming to Fulton Market. Friday."), social and email reveal the details, and the truck returns on launch day with the full message and a QR code.
Event surround
The truck works the streets outside a game, festival or convention; social and search target the venue area during the event; email the next morning thanks attendees with an offer.
A sample campaign week
Day Street Digital
Monday — Email teaser to customers
Tuesday Truck: commute and lunch routes Social teaser in the same ZIP codes
Wednesday — Search ads on brand terms; retarget site visitors
Thursday Truck: lunch and evening routes CTV in the same areas
Friday Truck: launch or event day Social with the offer; search on brand terms
Saturday The truck in shopping districts and crowds Social retargeting
Sunday — Email recap with a code
Rules that keep it working
Match place and time. Digital follow-up should target the areas the truck drove, during the same days.
Keep one idea. Same line, same visual, same colors on the street and in the feed.
Adapt the format. The truck needs five to seven words; social can carry the details.
One code per channel. Separate QR codes, promo codes or phone numbers so you can tell them apart.
Don't change everything at once. Change one channel at a time between flights so you can see what moved the result.
Reading results across the plan
Out-of-home often shows up in other channels' numbers: more brand searches, more direct visits, better social response in the areas the truck ran. Read the plan as a whole: total responses, brand-search volume and sales in exposed areas compared with a baseline and a similar unexposed area, alongside each channel's own code.
How AOTC plugs into the plan
AOTC plans the street side by daypart, designs creative that matches your campaign, and sends a GPS-tracked route and photos after every run, so your digital team knows exactly which neighborhoods and hours to follow up. Standard bookings are rotational, with no competitor in your rotation. Related reading: how to add OOH to a digital plan and geographic targeting for local campaigns .

### Mobile LED public awareness campaigns in 2026 (https://adsofthecentury.net/mobile-led-public-awareness-campaigns.html)
Key takeaways:
Give the campaign one ask: call, get screened, sign up, show up or vote.
Route to the communities the message is for, at the hours people are out.
Run the message in the languages those communities speak.
Photos of the screen in public extend an awareness campaign through press and social.
Issue and political ads may need a 'paid for by' line; check the rules that apply.
Who runs awareness campaigns on the street
Organization Typical ask
Nonprofits Call a hotline, find a service, donate, volunteer
Public health and hospitals Get screened, get vaccinated, know the warning signs
Labor unions Support a contract fight, end a lockout, join
Advocacy groups Show up to a hearing or rally, contact an official
Government agencies Safety, recruitment, census, program enrollment
Election campaigns Register, vote early, vote on the day
One ask, said plainly
A moving screen gives people a few seconds. Use them for one action and the way to take it: "Struggling? Call or text 988." "Free screenings Saturday at Union Park." "Vote early at your library." Leave the explanation for the website the QR code opens.
Take it to the people it's for
Awareness messages fail when they reach everyone except the audience they're for. Route the truck through the specific neighborhoods, worksites, campuses or corridors where that audience lives and works, at the hours they're out: shift changes, school pickup, weekend shopping, evening commute.
Speak every community's language
Alternate English with Spanish, Polish, Chinese, Arabic or whatever the route calls for. A digital screen can switch language within one loop, or change it by neighborhood as the route moves.
Presence is part of the message
For causes and campaigns, being seen in public is a statement in itself: a lockout message outside headquarters, a mental-health message during a festival weekend, a rally reminder outside city hall. Photos of the screen in those places travel through press and social and extend the campaign far beyond the street.
Disclosure and rules
Political and issue ads may require a "paid for by" line naming the sponsor under federal or state law.
Health claims should match the guidance of the responsible agency.
Vehicle rules: AOTC checks each city's rules for advertising vehicles before the truck rolls.
Confirm disclosure wording with your counsel or compliance team.
Measuring awareness
Count the ask: calls, texts, sign-ups, screenings or attendance from a number or link only the screens use.
Compare with a baseline: the same weeks before the campaign.
Survey at scale: a short recall survey in reached and unreached areas.
Track earned reach: press mentions and social posts showing the screen.
How AOTC runs awareness campaigns
AOTC has run labor and mental-health awareness campaigns from Northwest Indiana to downtown Chicago. We plan routes to the communities the message is for, design creative in-house in the languages needed, and send a GPS-tracked route and photos after every run. ### Outdoor advertising for Gen Z in 2026 (https://adsofthecentury.net/gen-z-outdoor-advertising-2026.html)
Key takeaways:
Plan Gen Z outdoor by place and hour: campuses, transit, venues and nightlife.
Evenings and weekends matter more than the morning commute for this audience.
Moving formats such as mobile LED trucks follow the crowd from venue to venue.
Run social in the same areas and days so the street ad gets a second exposure.
Measure QR scans, social mentions, creator posts and brand search, not just impressions.
Where and when Gen Z is outdoors
Place When Format that fits
College campuses Class changes, lunch, move-in week Mobile LED on the edge of campus
Transit hubs Afternoon and evening Station screens, mobile LED on nearby streets
Concerts and festivals Gates open and letting out Mobile LED trucks by the gates and crowd zones
Game days Before first pitch or kickoff, after the final out Mobile LED around the stadium
Nightlife districts 9 p.m. to late Mobile LED, which reads brightest after dark
Gyms, coffee, shopping streets Afternoons and weekends Place-based screens, mobile LED on the shopping streets
Build around the cultural calendar
The biggest Gen Z moments are dated: move-in week, homecoming, festival weekends, playoff runs, spring break, graduation. In Chicago, Lollapalooza in Grant Park (late July or August), Cubs games in Wrigleyville and the city's neighborhood street festivals each concentrate young crowds in a few blocks for a few hours. Book those dates early; demand for street time peaks with the crowd.
Why moving formats suit this audience
They follow the crowd. A truck can be at the campus at noon and the concert at 10 p.m.
They're at eye level. Street-level screens feel more like part of the scene than a board overhead.
They move. Full-motion video holds attention and gets filmed.
They can change. Different lines for the game, the after-party and the next morning.
Pair the street with social
Run social in the same ZIP codes and on the same days as the outdoor flight, with the same creative idea. Seed the moment: have your team or a few creators film the screen and post it. Repost the best fan clips. The street ad gives social something real to talk about; social carries it past the block it ran on.
What to measure
QR scans by hour and location
Social mentions, tags and creator posts that show the screen
Brand search and app-store searches in the cities that ran
Sign-ups or sales with a code only the outdoor ad used
How AOTC reaches Gen Z on the street

### Personal injury law firm advertising beyond billboards (https://adsofthecentury.net/personal-injury-advertising-beyond-billboards.html)
Key takeaways:
Billboards build recall; the rest of the mix catches people when they're ready to call.
Search and Local Services Ads reach people actively looking for a lawyer, at the highest intent.
TV, CTV and audio build the name broadly; mobile LED does it street by street.
Sponsorships and community presence build trust that ads alone don't.
Track every channel with its own number or link, and ask every caller where they heard of you.
The mix, compared
Channel Role Measure by Watch out for
Highway billboards Long-term recall on major roads Calls to a board-only number Long contracts, one location
TV and CTV Broad recall, the firm's face and voice Call spikes after airings, a TV-only number Production cost, frequency needed
Radio and streaming audio Commuters and workers on the job A memorable number or vanity URL Recall without a visual
Search ads and Local Services Ads People actively looking Leads and signed cases per dollar High competition, lead quality
SEO and content Search presence that compounds Organic leads over months Slow to build
Social Community reach, education, reviews Leads from social forms and calls Ad rules apply to posts too
Sponsorships Local goodwill and visibility Mentions, branded searches Hard to measure directly
Mobile LED Street-level presence in the communities served Calls to a screen-only number, area lift Placement must stay tasteful
Referrals Cases from other lawyers and past clients Referral source in intake Referral-fee rules vary by state
Recall channels and intent channels
Think of the mix in two halves. Recall channels (billboards, TV, CTV, audio, mobile LED, sponsorships) make the firm's name the one people remember. Intent channels (search, Local Services Ads, SEO) catch people at the moment they're looking. Recall makes intent cheaper: someone who already knows the firm's name searches for it, instead of clicking whichever ad is on top.
Community presence
Personal injury clients often choose a firm that feels like part of their community. Sponsoring youth sports, showing up at neighborhood festivals and running ads in the languages people speak build that feeling. A mobile LED screen can take the firm's message to the same neighborhoods, at the hours people are out, with the message in English and Spanish in the same loop.
Measuring the whole mix
One tracking number or link per channel.
Ask every caller where they heard of the firm, and record it in intake.
Judge by signed cases, not calls or clicks.
Watch branded search: it rises when recall channels work.
Compare areas: call volume from neighborhoods the street media reached vs. similar ones it didn't.
The rules cover everything
Each state's rules of professional conduct govern a lawyer's communications in every medium. Truthful, not misleading, a responsible lawyer or firm identified, and state-specific requirements on labels, testimonials and past results. Have counsel review new creative in any channel.
Where AOTC fits a law firm's mix
AOTC adds the street-level piece: tasteful routes through the communities a firm serves, creative designed in-house for the firm's review, no competing firm in the rotation, and a GPS-tracked route and photos after every run. ### Restaurant grand opening marketing for franchisees (https://adsofthecentury.net/restaurant-grand-opening-marketing-franchisees.html)
Key takeaways:
Get local creative approved early; franchisors often have brand standards and review times for local ads.
Local store marketing budgets and ad co-op funds may cover opening media; check your agreement.
Start about six weeks out: hiring, signage, community, soft opening, opening week.
The trade area for a restaurant is usually the commute, lunch and dinner paths around the site.
Measure opening-week transactions, sign-ups and code redemptions against the brand's typical opening.
Start with the franchisor's rules
Franchisees get a recognized brand, and with it a rulebook. Before planning any local media:
Read the marketing manual. Logo use, colors, fonts, approved offers and required legal lines.
Learn the approval process. Many systems review local ads; build their turnaround time into the schedule.
Check what's funded. Grand opening kits, local store marketing (LSM) budgets and ad co-op funds may cover part of the opening. Find out which channels qualify.
Ask for the opening playbook. Systems that open many locations often have a proven sequence and benchmarks.
A six-week opening timeline
When What happens
6 weeks out Hiring signage, "coming soon" banner, local listings created, creative submitted for approval
4 weeks out Community outreach: schools, offices, the chamber of commerce, nearby businesses
2 weeks out Social and email teasers in the trade area; mobile billboard route planned
1 week out Teaser run on the screens: "Opening Friday on Main Street"
Soft opening Friends-and-family or invite-only service to train the crew
Opening week Truck on opening day and the first weekend; giveaways; local press invited
2 weeks after Second wave aimed at lunch and dinner regulars; review the numbers
Know the restaurant's trade area
A restaurant's customers mostly come from the paths people already travel: the commute past the site, the offices and schools within a short drive at lunch, and the homes nearby at dinner. Map those paths, then put the opening's most visible media on them at the right hours.
Local tactics that fill the dining room
A mobile LED billboard around the trade area on opening day and the first weekend, parked or circling where it's allowed.
App or loyalty sign-up offers with a QR code, so new guests become repeat guests.
Community first-day perks: first responders, teachers or the first hundred guests.
Local press and creators invited to the soft opening.
Neighbor businesses: a coupon for staff at nearby offices and shops.
What to measure
Opening-week transactions against the brand's typical new-store opening
App downloads and loyalty sign-ups from the opening QR code
Redemptions of the opening offer
Week two and week four transactions: did the opening build regulars?

### Seasonal outdoor advertising for home services (https://adsofthecentury.net/seasonal-home-services-advertising.html)
Key takeaways:
Each trade has a peak season; advertise just before it and through it.
Trigger moments (first heat wave, first freeze, big storms) create sudden demand worth being ready for.
Book the planned seasonal bursts early and keep a few flexible days for triggers.
Change the message with the weather: tune-up offers before the peak, fast service during it.
Track calls by week and compare each season with the same season last year.
The season-by-season calendar
Season Trades at peak Message
Spring Roofing, gutters, landscaping, lawn care, AC tune-ups, windows "Book before the rush"
Summer AC repair, decks and patios, pest control, pools, painting "Same-week service"
Fall Furnace tune-ups, roofing and gutters before winter, insulation, windows "Get ready for winter"
Winter Furnace repair, frozen and burst pipes, snow removal, indoor remodels "24/7 emergency service"
Trigger moments
Demand for some trades jumps overnight when the weather turns. Be ready for:
The first heat wave: AC repair and installs.
The first hard freeze: furnace repair, frozen pipes, water heaters.
Hail, wind and heavy storms: roofing, siding, gutters, tree work, water damage.
The first big snow: plowing and snow removal.
Spring thaw and heavy rain: basements, sump pumps, waterproofing.
Keep trigger creative designed and approved in advance, so you can add street days quickly when the moment comes.
Plan the year in bursts
Mark your trade's peak weeks from last year's call volume.
Book planned bursts just before and during those weeks.
Keep flexible days in the budget for trigger moments.
Run lighter maintenance messages in the off-season to past customers and nearby neighborhoods.
Where to run seasonal outdoor ads
The neighborhoods that hire you most, by ZIP code
Commuter corridors into those neighborhoods at rush hour
Home-improvement store and shopping-center traffic on weekends
Storm-affected areas after severe weather, with a helpful, not pushy, message
Measure season over season
Track calls and booked jobs by week, with a phone number only the outdoor ads use. Compare each season with the same season last year, and note the weather; a mild summer and a hot one aren't comparable without it.

### Tech brand launch billboard campaigns (https://adsofthecentury.net/tech-brand-launch-billboard-campaigns.html)
Key takeaways:
Build each launch billboard around one idea, one place and one day.
Countdowns and reveals use the LED screen's ability to change message over time.
Conference takeovers concentrate budget where the buyers already are.
A QR code to a waitlist or download makes the street a measurable channel.
Comparative or competitor-adjacent ideas need a legal review before they run.
Eight campaign ideas
Idea On the screen Best for Measure
Countdown teaser "3 days." "2 days." "Tomorrow." Then the reveal Consumer launches, big reveals Waitlist sign-ups, search lift
Conference takeover The product outside the venue, all show week B2B software, developer tools Demo requests, booth traffic
Street demo The product doing one thing, big, in motion Apps, devices, visual products QR scans, downloads
Hometown launch "Built in Chicago. Live today." Startups, local tech Local press, local sign-ups
Multi-city drop The same reveal in several cities on one day National consumer launches Search lift by city
QR waitlist race "First 1,000 scans get early access" Apps with a waitlist Scans, sign-ups by hour
Inside joke A line only developers or the industry will get Developer and B2B audiences Social shares in the community
Thank-you lap "Thanks, Austin. See you next year." After a conference or launch Recall, follow-up conversions
The countdown: use time as the idea
A static board can't count down; an LED screen can. Run the teaser on the same routes each day with the number changing, so regulars on those streets notice the progression, then reveal on launch day. Keep the brand visible throughout so the search works.
The conference takeover: go where the buyers are
For B2B launches, the conference is the market. Route the truck between the venue entrances, the official hotels and the evening events, timed to the keynote and session breaks, and change the message by audience: technical in the morning, business value at lunch, the after-party invite at night.
The street demo: show one thing
Full-motion screens can show the product working at a size that stops people: the interface doing the one thing it does best, the device from every angle, the before and after. One action per loop, no feature lists.
The hometown launch: local pride as reach
Local tech companies have an advantage national brands don't: the city is proud of them. A launch message that names the neighborhood or the city earns local press and goodwill, and it reads as confident rather than corporate.
Rules for every launch campaign
One idea per campaign, five to seven words on screen at a time.
The brand must be legible in a phone photo, because that's how the ad travels.
A next step people can take there: a QR code they can scan from the sidewalk, or a short URL.
Search ready: paid search and the landing page live before the first screen lights up.
Legal review for any comparative claim or competitor reference.

Budgeting the launch
Published industry rate guides put an LED billboard truck at roughly $1,200 to $3,600 per day, usually with a minimum of about four hours, and big event weeks can cost more. Concentrate the budget on launch day and the busiest conference days rather than spreading it evenly. For a smaller budget, share the truck in a rotation with non-competing brands instead of booking it exclusively.

Waitlist sign-ups, downloads or demo requests from the screens' QR code
Brand and product search volume during launch week vs. the weeks before
Direct site traffic from the launch cities
Press and social mentions that include photos of the screens

### The complete guide to OOH sales attribution (https://adsofthecentury.net/ooh-sales-attribution-guide.html)
Key takeaways:
No single method proves everything; combine a direct-response code with a comparison against areas the ad didn't reach.
Response codes are cheap and exact, but they undercount: many people who act never scan or type the code.
Matched-market tests are the most convincing method for local budgets: change one thing in one area and compare.
Mix models and mobile location studies need scale, history and careful privacy handling.
A GPS-tracked route with times is what lets you line sales up with where and when the ad actually ran.
Why OOH attribution takes a plan
A digital ad leaves a trail: a click, a cookie, a conversion pixel. A street screen doesn't. Someone sees it at a red light, remembers the name two days later and searches for it on a phone, and no system connects the two by itself. Attribution for out-of-home is the work of building that connection on purpose, before the campaign starts.
The methods, compared
Method What it shows Best for Watch out for
Response codes Exact actions from the ad: scans, code uses, calls Every campaign Undercounts people who act another way
Search and site lift More brand searches and visits where the ad ran Launches, new brands Other marketing in the same weeks
Matched-market test Sales or calls in exposed areas vs. similar unexposed ones Local and regional budgets Areas that aren't really alike
Brand lift survey Awareness and recall, exposed vs. not Awareness goals, causes Small samples; recall isn't a sale
Mobile location study Store visits by devices seen near the route Retail with many locations Panel size, consent and privacy rules
Marketing mix model Each channel's share of sales over time Large, steady budgets Needs years of data and an analyst
Response codes: the floor
Start every campaign with a response path nobody else uses: a QR code large enough to scan from the sidewalk, a short promo code, a vanity URL or a dedicated phone number. These count real people taking a real step. They also undercount, because many people who act on an outdoor ad simply search the brand name later. Report them as the minimum the campaign produced.
Matched-market tests: the strongest local method
Choose two areas that behave alike: similar neighborhoods, similar stores, similar sales history. Run the campaign in one. Keep pricing, promotions and other media the same in both. Then compare each area's change against its own baseline. If the exposed area grows and the control area doesn't, the difference is your best estimate of lift. Our step-by-step version is in how to measure OOH sales lift with GPS route data .
Mobile data and mix models
Location studies match devices seen near a route with later store visits. They can work for chains with many locations, but they depend on panel size and on handling consent and privacy correctly. Marketing mix models estimate every channel's contribution from years of spend and sales data. Both are worth it at scale; for a single opening or a month of local presence, a code plus a matched-market test usually tells you more for less.
Five mistakes that ruin attribution
Sharing one promo code across radio, social and the truck.
Changing prices or running a big promotion in the test area only.
Comparing against the campaign's own dashboard instead of a baseline.
Picking a "control" area the campaign also drove through.
Reading the result after two days instead of the full window customers need to act.
What AOTC brings to the comparison
Attribution needs to know exactly where and when the ad ran. AOTC sends a GPS-tracked route with times and photos of the ad on the street after every run, shows the truck live in the Golden Ticket route room, and estimates impressions with the same conservative method on every route. For a clean test, book exclusively so the truck carries only your brand. Your sales, calls and site data complete the picture, and we'll help plan the test and control areas before the first day. ### The complete guide to real estate development ads (https://adsofthecentury.net/real-estate-development-advertising.html)
Key takeaways:
Plan development advertising in five phases, each with its own message and goal.
Pre-launch builds the interest list; everything after converts it into appointments and contracts.
Reach likely buyers or renters where they live and work now, not only near the site.
Fair-housing law prohibits ads that state or imply a preference based on protected characteristics.
Street-level screens fit launch events, groundbreaking, open houses and commuter routes to the site.
The five phases
Phase Goal Main message Channels
Pre-launch An interest list "Coming to [neighborhood]. Register." Site signage, search, social, street screens near the site
Launch and pre-sales / pre-leasing Sales-center appointments "Now selling" or "Now leasing," the price range, the incentive Launch event, street screens on commuter routes, email, social
Construction Momentum and trust Progress, milestones, units remaining Site fencing, social, email, the topping-out event
Opening Tours and move-ins "Now open. Tour today." Open houses, street screens, search
Sell-out or lease-up The last units "Final units," the incentive Targeted digital, broker outreach, open houses
Who you're selling to
Buyers or renters moving within the city, reached where they live and commute now.
People relocating for work, reached near major employers and through relocation channels.
Downsizers, reached in established neighborhoods nearby.
Brokers and agents, who bring many buyers; reach them with broker events and incentives.
Investors, for some product types.
Where street-level screens fit
Groundbreaking and launch events: the screen on site, showing renderings and the register link.
Commuter routes: the corridors likely buyers use every day, at rush hour.
Feeder neighborhoods: where today's renters and owners live, on weekends.
Open houses: the truck routing traffic to the tour, with directions.
Renderings and video tours play well on full-motion LED screens; keep the words to the project name, the neighborhood and one action.
The rules
Fair housing. The federal Fair Housing Act bars advertising that states or implies a preference or limitation based on protected characteristics; many states and cities protect additional classes. Watch imagery and wording, and include the equal housing opportunity logo or statement.
Licensing. If licensees market the units, state license law usually requires the brokerage's name in the ad.
Accurate claims. Renderings, prices, amenities and completion dates must be accurate and qualified where needed.
Have counsel or the managing broker review campaign creative.
Measuring development marketing
Interest-list sign-ups by source
Sales or leasing-center appointments and tours
Contracts or signed leases by source
Cost per appointment and cost per contract by channel
How AOTC supports developments
AOTC brings renderings and launch messages to the street: on site at groundbreaking and launch events, and on the commuter routes and feeder neighborhoods where your buyers or renters are now. Creative is designed in-house for your review, and every run comes with a GPS-tracked route and photos. ### Understanding geographic targeting for local campaigns (https://adsofthecentury.net/geographic-targeting-local-campaigns.html)
Key takeaways:
Targeting by place works best when the trade area comes from real customer data, not a guess.
Radius and ZIP targeting are simple; geofences and venues are precise; routes add time of day.
A DMA is a TV market, often far bigger than a local business needs.
Mobile billboards target by street and hour, which digital geo-targeting can't do on its own.
Combining a physical route with a digital geofence reaches the same area twice, in two ways.
The types of geographic targeting
Type How it works Good for Limits
Radius A circle around an address Simple local search and social ads Circles ignore rivers, highways and habits
ZIP or postal code Chosen postal areas Direct mail, social, CTV Large or oddly shaped areas
DMA A TV market Regional TV, CTV, radio Usually far too big for one location
Geofence A drawn boundary for mobile devices Competitor sites, events, campuses Location-data accuracy and privacy rules
Venue Screens or ads tied to specific places Stadiums, malls, airports, gyms Only where screens or data exist
Route A mobile billboard drives chosen streets by hour Neighborhoods, events, openings, districts One vehicle covers one route at a time
Draw the trade area first
Map real customers. Pull ZIP codes or addresses from sales, bookings or loyalty data.
Find the clusters. Customers rarely spread evenly; they bunch in a few areas.
Add their day. Where do those people commute, work, eat, shop and go out?
Mark the barriers. Highways, rivers and rail lines change how far people travel.
Note the competitors. Areas close to a rival may need more presence, or none.
Place is only half of it: add time
The same block holds different people at 8 a.m., noon and 10 p.m. Digital geo-targeting answers "where is the device?" A planned route answers "where is the audience right now?" In Chicago, for example, that means the Loop and West Loop for the morning commute, the Magnificent Mile and River North at midday, Wrigleyville or Soldier Field on game days, and River North and Fulton Market after dark.
Combining physical and digital targeting
Route plus geofence. Drive the truck through a neighborhood, and geofence the same area for mobile ads that follow up.
Route plus search. Expect brand searches to rise where the truck ran; make sure local search ads and listings are ready.
Route plus social. Run social ads in the same ZIP codes during the same days, so the message lands twice.
More on sequencing in mobile LED DOOH for omnichannel media plans .
Common targeting mistakes
Using a round radius when customers come from one direction.
Buying a whole DMA for a single store.
Targeting where people live but advertising at hours they're at work.
Changing the area mid-campaign, which makes results impossible to read.
How AOTC targets by street and hour
AOTC plans every route from your trade area and the audience's day, checks each city's rules for advertising vehicles, and sends a GPS-tracked route and photos after every run, so you can see exactly where the ad went. That route record is also what makes a sales-lift test possible. See markets on the nationwide page or start with Chicago .

### Understanding OOH in a digital media plan (https://adsofthecentury.net/ooh-in-digital-media-plan.html)
Key takeaways:
OOH works at the top and middle of the funnel: awareness, consideration and the nudge to visit.
Its audiences are estimated from location data; digital audiences are counted but can include invalid traffic.
Planners compare both with reach, frequency and CPM, then cost per response.
OOH's effect often appears in other channels first, as more brand searches and direct visits.
OOH can't take the click; plan the digital follow-up so the interest it creates has somewhere to go.
OOH's role in the funnel
Digital channels are strongest near the bottom of the funnel, where someone is already searching, comparing or ready to buy. Out-of-home is strongest near the top and middle: making a brand familiar, making a launch feel big, and reminding people near a store, venue or event that it's there.
Awareness. Everyone on the street sees it, including people who skip or block online ads.
Consideration. Seeing a brand in the real world makes it feel established and local.
The nudge. A screen outside the venue or two blocks from the store tips the decision in the moment.
How each side counts its audience
Out-of-home Digital
Impressions Estimated from traffic, foot counts or location data Counted by ad servers and platforms
Main risk Estimates that are generous or unexplained Invalid traffic and ads nobody saw
Skippable? No Often
Clickable? No (QR codes and URLs bridge the gap) Yes
Where results show Search, direct visits, calls, store sales Clicks and conversions
The planning terms, in plain English
Impressions: opportunities to see the ad.
Reach: how many different people had at least one opportunity.
Frequency: how many times, on average, each of them had one.
CPM: cost per thousand impressions, the price of reach.
Share of voice: your share of the screen time or the category's ads. In an AOTC rotation it runs from about 15% to 100%, and an exclusive booking is 100%.
Daypart: a time block, such as morning commute or late night.
Lift: the extra searches, visits or sales in exposed areas compared with a baseline.
The halo: why OOH shows up in other channels
Someone sees a truck at a red light, doesn't scan anything, and searches the brand that evening. The out-of-home ad did the work, and the search ad gets the credit. That's why OOH should be judged by what happens across the plan in the areas it ran: brand-search volume, direct traffic, calls and sales, compared with a baseline and, ideally, a similar area without the campaign.
What OOH can't do
Take a click or complete a purchase on its own.
Target one person by their browsing history.
Report a person-by-person count of who saw it.
Those limits are why the best plans pair it with digital follow-up: the street creates the interest, and search, social and the website catch it.
How AOTC plans OOH alongside digital
AOTC routes the truck through the places and hours your digital audiences live their day, designs creative that matches your campaign, and sends a GPS-tracked route and photos after every run, with estimated impressions worked out the same way every time. Next steps: how to add OOH to a digital media plan and mobile LED DOOH for omnichannel plans .

### What is bot-free advertising in 2026? (https://adsofthecentury.net/bot-free-advertising.html)
Key takeaways:
Invalid traffic (IVT) is any ad activity not made by a real, interested person; the industry splits it into general and sophisticated IVT.
One 2026 study of more than 2.7 billion paid clicks found roughly 8.5% of them invalid.
Physical media (billboards, mobile LED trucks, events, print) are bot-free by nature.
Digital media can be made cleaner, not bot-free: buy from authorized sellers and pay for outcomes.
Bot-free isn't the same as measured; check the method behind any audience number.
Bot-free, defined
An ad is bot-free when the thing you pay for (an impression, a view, a click) can only come from a person. That rules out most of the ways digital budgets get drained: crawlers that load pages, scripts that click ads, apps that pretend to be other apps, and ads stacked or hidden where nobody can see them.
The industry's name for the problem is invalid traffic, or IVT. Measurement standards split it in two:
General invalid traffic. Known crawlers, data-center traffic and obvious automation that standard filters remove.
Sophisticated invalid traffic. Bots built to look human, hijacked devices, spoofed apps and domains, which take deeper analysis to catch.
Why it matters more in 2026
Automation keeps getting cheaper. Lunio's 2026 Global Invalid Traffic Report, which analyzed more than 2.7 billion paid clicks across the major ad platforms, found roughly 8.5% of them invalid. At the same time, automated agents and scrapers browse more of the web on someone's behalf, and some of that activity can load ads. For a buyer, the result is the same: part of the bill is for an audience that never existed.
Which formats are bot-free by nature
Format Bot-free? Why
Mobile LED billboard Yes The audience is on the street; the route and photos are the record
Fixed billboard Yes A physical board with an audited audience
Events and sampling Yes People in the room
Print and direct mail Yes Physical copies delivered
Search and social No Clicks and views can be automated
Programmatic display and CTV No Impressions and devices can be spoofed
Digital channels can't be made bot-free, but they can be made cleaner: buy from authorized sellers, check placement lists, and pay for outcomes (calls, bookings, purchases) instead of impressions wherever you can.
Bot-free isn't the same as measured
A street screen can't be faked, but its audience is still an estimate. Before you compare a bot-free channel with anything else, ask three questions:
How was the audience worked out? A method you can read beats a round number.
What's the record? Photos, a GPS-tracked route, an audited board audience.
How will response be counted? A QR code, promo code, vanity URL or call-tracking number.
Where AOTC fits a bot-free plan
AOTC's LED billboard truck puts the ad in front of people on the street, at the hours they're there. Every run has a GPS-tracked route and photos, and impressions are estimated the same way every time: at least one viewer per second on screen, plus the audience of every Lamar and OUTFRONT billboard the route passes, for the minutes the vehicle is beside them. It's a number for planning, never presented as a guarantee.
See how that compares on price in mobile billboard CPM vs. CTV and social , or see how a booking is priced in the FAQ .

### What is driving DOOH growth in 2026? (https://adsofthecentury.net/dooh-growth-2026.html)
Key takeaways:
U.S. out-of-home revenue hit a record $9.46 billion in 2025, per the OAAA; digital was 36.3% of it and grew 10.5%.
Programmatic DOOH lets buyers add screens from the same tools they use for digital media.
Audience and location data make DOOH plannable and measurable like other channels.
Cookie loss and ad fatigue push budgets toward media that doesn't depend on tracking a person online.
Mobile LED is DOOH that moves: it goes where the audience is instead of waiting for it.
The numbers
According to the Out of Home Advertising Association of America (OAAA), U.S. out-of-home advertising revenue reached a record $9.46 billion in 2025, up 3.6% from the year before and extending a long run of quarterly growth. Digital out-of-home made up 36.3% of that total and grew 10.5%, roughly three times the pace of the market as a whole.
In other words, outdoor isn't just holding on in a digital-first world. Its digital half is where the growth is.
Five forces behind the growth
1. Buying got easier
Programmatic DOOH lets buyers add screens through the same platforms they use for display, video and CTV, with flexible budgets and short flights. That brings outdoor into plans that used to be digital-only.
2. Measurement caught up
Audience data, mobile location panels and response tools such as QR codes make DOOH plannable and readable the way other channels are. Buyers can compare it with the rest of the plan instead of treating it as a leap of faith.
3. Privacy changed the math
As third-party cookies fade and tracking gets harder, media that reaches people in a place, without following them online, looks more attractive. DOOH doesn't need anyone's browsing history to work.
4. Screens became flexible
A digital screen can show breakfast in the morning and the late-night menu after 10, change by neighborhood, or count down to an opening. Messages fit the moment instead of running unchanged for a month.
5. Outdoor feeds social
Big, unexpected screens get filmed. A clever placement can travel far beyond the street it ran on, which turns a local buy into content.
Where the growth shows up
Format What's new
Digital billboards Short flights and programmatic access instead of four-week contracts
Place-based screens Gyms, bars, stores and offices sold by audience and venue type
Retail screens In-store screens tied to retail media and sales data
Mobile LED billboards Screens that drive to the audience, by hour and neighborhood
What it means for advertisers
DOOH belongs in the media plan, not in a separate "brand" bucket. Plan it with the same audiences and goals as digital.
Short flights are normal now. You can buy a weekend, a game day or a single evening.
Measure it like everything else. A response code per channel and a comparison against a baseline.
Expect competition for the best moments. Big event weeks fill early; plan ahead.
Where AOTC fits
AOTC runs DOOH that moves: an LED billboard truck with two full-size side screens, a rear screen and a front screen. Standard truck bookings are rotational, with no competing brand in your rotation, and every booking comes with Golden Ticket access to watch the route live. For the playbook, see mobile LED DOOH campaigns for 2026 growth and the local DOOH media planning guide .

### What makes outdoor ads stick with Gen Z (https://adsofthecentury.net/outdoor-ads-gen-z-memory.html)
Key takeaways:
Gen Z remembers outdoor ads that feel like a moment, not a sales pitch.
Self-aware humor and plain honesty beat borrowed slang.
Naming the place, the event or the neighborhood makes the ad feel like it's for them.
Make it worth filming: motion, a reveal or a joke that lands in a phone frame.
Two-thirds of Gen Z and millennial respondents in a 2021 OAAA and Harris Poll survey recalled seeing OOH ads on social media.
Why Gen Z is a hard audience, and a good one
Gen Z has skippable ads, ad blockers and endless feeds. They've learned to tune advertising out. That's exactly why outdoor matters: it's one of the few places an ad can't be skipped. But not being skippable only gets a glance. Getting remembered takes creative that earns the second look.
Six traits of outdoor ads that stick
1. It feels like a moment
The ad that shows up outside the concert as the crowd lets out, or names the game in progress, feels like part of the night instead of an interruption. Timing and place do half the creative work.
2. It's honest, and a little self-aware
A brand that admits it's an ad, or jokes about itself, reads as confident. Borrowed slang and fake authenticity read as trying too hard.
3. It's specific
Naming the neighborhood, the campus, the train line or the event tells people the ad was made for them. Generic national lines are easy to ignore.
4. It moves
A reveal, a countdown or a loop that rewards watching to the end holds attention on a full-motion LED screen in a way a static board can't.
5. It's worth filming
If someone would pull out a phone to show a friend, the ad keeps working long after the truck drives on. Design so the joke and the brand both fit in a phone frame.
6. It's easy to act on
A QR code big enough to scan, a handle or a short URL. No paragraph of instructions.
What makes Gen Z look away
Slang that's already dated by the time the ad runs
Feature lists and fine print
Brand logos with no idea attached
Claims that sound too good to be true
The same ad, unchanged, in every city and every hour
The social afterlife
Outdoor and social aren't separate for Gen Z. In a 2021 survey by the OAAA and The Harris Poll, two-thirds of Gen Z and millennial respondents said they recalled seeing outdoor ads on social media. A street ad that's filmed and posted reaches far more people than the ones who were standing there. Plan for it: make the ad worth posting, and repost the best clips yourself.
Turning the traits into lines
Trait Weak Stronger
Moment "Great food, great prices" "Lolla's over. Tacos aren't. Two blocks east."
Honesty "The best app ever" "It's a budgeting app. It's boring. Your bank account won't be."
Specific "Now in Chicago" "Now open on Milwaukee Ave. Yes, that one."
How AOTC makes ads that stick
AOTC designs full-motion creative in-house for the truck's screens and plans routes around the campuses, venues and nightlife districts where young audiences are, at the hours they're there. Every run comes with a GPS-tracked route and photos, which double as content. For the media plan, read outdoor advertising for Gen Z in 2026 ; for design, mobile LED ads built for social sharing .

### What personal injury firms should know about mobile LED (https://adsofthecentury.net/personal-injury-mobile-led-guide.html)
Key takeaways:
Lawyer-advertising rules apply to every screen: truthful, not misleading, with a responsible lawyer or firm identified.
Never route or park near accident scenes, emergency rooms or funerals; it's distasteful and can raise solicitation concerns.
The creative's job is recall: the firm name, the practice area and a number or short web address.
Run in the languages of the communities you serve.
A dedicated call-tracking number is the simplest way to see what the screens produce.
1. The advertising rules apply on every screen
Lawyer advertising is regulated by each state's rules of professional conduct, most of them modeled on the ABA Model Rules. In general:
No false or misleading communications (Model Rule 7.1), including implied guarantees of results.
Identify who's responsible: the name and contact information of at least one lawyer or firm (Model Rule 7.2).
Limits on solicitation of specific people (Model Rule 7.3).
State extras: some states require labels, disclaimers on past results or restrict testimonials and dramatizations.
Have the firm's ethics counsel or your state bar's advertising guidance check the creative. This guide isn't legal advice.
2. Placement must be tasteful
A truck can go almost anywhere, which is exactly why firms need a rule: never near accident scenes, emergency rooms, hospitals or funerals. Beyond being distasteful, appearing where people are in crisis can look like targeting specific victims. Route on commuter corridors, arterials and community streets instead.
3. Recall is the creative's job
People rarely need a lawyer the moment they see the ad. They need to remember the firm when they do. That means:
The firm name, large
The practice area in a few words ("Injured at work?")
An easy number or short web address, held on screen long enough to remember
Consistency with the firm's TV, radio and highway boards, so every exposure builds the same memory
4. Language and community
Serve communities in the languages they speak. A digital screen can alternate English and Spanish (or Polish, or another language) in the same loop. Routes through the neighborhoods the firm serves, at the hours people are out, beat a generic downtown loop.
5. How it differs from a highway billboard
Highway billboard Mobile LED
Where One spot on one road Chosen streets and neighborhoods, by hour
Commitment Usually four weeks or more Hours or days
Message One, until reprinted (static) Can change by daypart or language
Share of screen Yours (static) or rotating (digital) Rotates with no competing firm; or yours alone on an exclusive booking
6. Cost
Published industry rate guides put an LED billboard truck at roughly $1,200 to $3,600 per day, usually with a four-hour minimum. AOTC quotes the exact route and hours, usually the same day.
7. Track the calls
Use a call-tracking number only the screens show, ask every caller where they heard of the firm, and compare call volume from the areas the truck drove with the weeks before. AOTC's GPS-tracked route shows exactly where and when the ad ran.
How AOTC works with law firms
AOTC plans tasteful routes through the communities a firm serves, designs creative in-house for the firm's compliance review, and sends a GPS-tracked route and photos after every run. For a campaign plan see mobile LED ads for personal injury law firms ; for the wider mix, personal injury advertising beyond billboards .
